utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters and to the court reporters. We can now resume our work. According to what we were told yesterday by both parties, we would like to welcome Mr. Kehoe back, and a large number of witnesses we're going to hear today, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One, I believe, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then we're going to hear the one witness. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. The witness this morning is Dr. Colin Kaiser from UNESCO and Dr. Kaiser's testimony will focus on the destruction of sacral and cultural monuments and for the most part Islamic sacral and cultural monuments that were destroyed in the Lasva valley area, Busovaca area as well as the Kiseljak area. Dr. Kaiser has been studying this subject for sometime, in the former Yugoslavia since the early '90s. During that period of time, he was assigned by the council of Europe to do a series of studies on the destruction of sacral and cultural monuments throughout the former Yugoslavia and the impact that destruction had on the various ethnic cultures who suffered that damage. He will explain to Your Honours, with some of the photographs that are in evidence, and a sampling of photographs that have not been received into evidence, exactly what the various religious, sacral or cultural structures are used for, why it is that one would destroy this type of structure, and the impact, again, on the ethnic group, in this case, the Muslim ethnic group, of such destruction. He will likewise offer some conclusions on what the entity in this case, the HVO, might be attempting to accomplish by such a destruction of Islamic sacral and cultural institutions. His presentation will focus, in the main, on two counts, and that count is count 1, the persecution count which, of course, encompasses as part of it, the destruction -- persecution of the Bosnian Muslim population in Central Bosnia and as a method of doing that, the destruction of their sacral and cultural monuments, and in the main count 14, which is a list of various cultural and sacral monuments in Kizeljak, Busovaca and Vitez that were destroyed by the HVO during the operative time frame. That will essentially be Dr. Kaiser's testimony, beginning with some background and moving down to the specifics as he goes through the pictures. I think it might be somewhat more efficient, Mr. President, if the photographs that have been provided to Mr. Dubuisson could be marked and be given to Dr. Kaiser so that he might begin his testimony to Your Honour and move these photographs on and off the ELMO as he sees fit. If there's no objection with the court, that might be a more efficient method to employ. And certainly, giving the new photographs to Defence council at this point, is perfectly appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This doesn't cause any problems for the Judges. Does it cause any problems for Mr. Hayman? Very well. All right. We can work that way. Registrar, have the usher bring Dr. Kaiser into the courtroom, please. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, we have to ask you to remain standing for a few moments. Please, put your headset on and we ask you to remain standing for a few moments. First of all, to confirm your title, your family name, your given name and then to read your solemn declaration. First give us your title, then your family name and -- we have to know who you are first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dr. Colin Kaiser. I'm the UNESCO representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now please read the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated now. You have been called by the Prosecution as part of the trial of Colonel Blaskic, the accused who is in this courtroom. The Prosecutor has given us a quick summary of the general sense of your testimony, and he will now ask you some questions after which, of course, you will be asked some questions by the Defence and by the Judges. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Dr. Kaiser. Mr. Kaiser, before we begin your testimony, can you tell the Judges a little bit about yourself, your educational background, your professional background, and I know that you noted that you are UNESCO's representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina at this point. You could tell the Judges what that exactly means.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I'm a social and institutional historian by training, a specialist in old regime France. Most of my professional life has not been involved directly in history, in any exercise and practice of history. I have worked in the International Council Monuments and Sites where I became director, so my main interest over the past ten years, really, has been cultural heritage. I passed from the International Council Monuments and Sites to UNESCO where I worked for them as a consultant in cultural heritage. In October 1995, when the cease-fire began in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was asked by UNESCO to take up the post of representative in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the head of mission, the chief of office, so I'm now responsible for carrying out, elaborating sometimes UNESCO projects in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in education, in cultural heritage, in media. I spent a lot of time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia during the wars. I'm spending a lot of time in Bosnia now hoping to see the pieces of the society come back together, to see it reconstructed. It's a very important job for me, privately. When you have seen things come apart, it's nice to see them come back together and try to contribute to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your work in UNESCO, you have been called to the Tribunal here in The Hague to testify before, have you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us just discuss for a moment what you said at the outset, and if you could again explain to the Judges your involvement in the study of sacral and cultural monuments in the former Yugoslavia, through the beginning of your work with the council of Europe, and if you could then explain to the Judges, as we move from the general to the more specific, the prescription of your work, how you do your work now, and if you could move down to the level of destruction of sacral and cultural monuments in Central Bosnia, and specifically areas under HVO control. Could you do that for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes. It began, in fact, with UNESCO, because I was one of two UNESCO observers sent to Dubrovnik in November and December of 1991. I was present in Dubrovnik during the Saint Nicholas Day bombardment on the 6th of December. It was quite a terrifying experience. It was a very eye opening experience, in the sense that the destruction, the bombardment of cultural and religious objects, the attack on the city which was completely defenceless seemed to me a very novel way to wage war. When the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina began, the fear, the sentiment that I had that this was a war which was not just about taking military objectives in the strict sense of the term, but these were wars about perhaps of identity which means that other things were also being targeted. It was very clear to us that the international community, at the beginning of the Bosnian war, wasn't very interested in these things. There was some sort of information from Sarajevo when the Vijecnica, the national university library, was set on fire, and that was kind of an archetypal crime against cultural heritage. But considering that the war was all over the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was great concern, at least in small circles, that, in fact, it was the military actions or post-military actions were taking place against the symbols of peoples' identity. My work with the council of Europe began merely in -- it began in the summer of 1992, but the first time we were able to go on mission was in November of 1992. It was extremely hard to go on mission because none of the international community would say that it's a proper mandate. UNPROFOR didn't have a mandate for cultural heritage. The European community monitoring mission didn't have a mandate for it. The UNHCR didn't have a mandate for it. So it took awhile to get into the field. The first mission was in Neretva valley. This, in some ways, was even more frightening and awesome than the mission in the Dubrovnik area because the amount of damage, for example, done to Mostar in the first battle of Mostar, by the Bosnian- Serbian army, in the period of three months, was really quite astounding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me a second. It's written here that the first mission was in Neretva valley. You mean Lasva valley? Neretva valley?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Neretva valley, the first mission for the council of Europe. Also, what was astounding was the reprisal activity. I had never seen a dynamited church. I had never seen a dynamited church from the 16th century, Zitomislic, which is an Orthodox monastery, or the new Orthodox church in Mostar, on the east side. This war was much more savage than the war that I had seen in the Dubrovnik commune. It took awhile to organise other missions. What I did mainly during 1993, was that I was recording information that was coming in, writing reports about what might be happening, with a sense of great frustration. There was some information that was filtering in. The destruction of the mosque in Banja Luka in May 1993. There was information about that. There was some sort of reaction to it. The destruction of the old bridge in Mostar in November 1993. That's another example where the international media became very interested, very briefly. In 1994, was the first time that Bosnia sort of came open to our activities. I was writing information reports for the council of Europe. The point of writing information reports was to hopefully build up some sort of reaction on the part of government members' states of the council of Europe, not so much public opinion. If you didn't have good information, you couldn't hope that your reports were going to have much of an impact. 1994, we had a very interesting echo from the European community monitoring commission. The sort of interest in what was going on came from the field, it came from the monitors themselves. They began to see in Bosnia that an awful lot of things were happening, and also in Croatia, and they were much more open to cooperating with the council of Europe than in the preceding years. So in March 1994, I carried out a mission in western Herzegovina and also parts of the United Nations protection areas. And then in May and June 1994, with European community monitoring mission, I carried out a mission in Central Bosnia. This was an important mission from the point of view of information. It covered the front zones between the Armija, the Bosnian Serbian army. It also concerned the Central Bosnia area, about which there was not so much information. Of course, we all heard about the Ahmici massacre in 1993. We had all sorts of rumours about other activities that had been carried out in the area, ethnic cleansing which was alleged. We had information that the Franciscan monastery in Guca Gora had been totally destroyed, that the great collections in the Franciscan monastery of Kraljeva Sutisca (phoen) had been totally dispersed, and this last case, if it was actually true, it would have been a very, very serious cultural loss. But the truth of the matter is, again, we knew nothing about it. Convoys were going everywhere. You see them all over the place. There's the other organs of the international community, but we didn't really know what was going on. So ECCM took me in, and concerning the areas which are of interest in the case against Mr. Blaskic, I did visit parts of the Vitez pocket. I was able to photograph a few buildings. I visited Busovaca. I went very quickly through the Kiseljak area, which was considered to be extremely dangerous. You couldn't even get out of the vehicle. You couldn't take pictures. That was the extent of my activity, in fact, in Central Bosnia, in this mission in 1994. I continued working after that. I worked in Mostar for UNESCO. I continued even in the rest of the war to do more small monitoring activities with ECMM which also set up their own monitoring system of cultural and sacral heritage. Also, in the post-war period, we continued to monitor churches and mosques because they continue, in periods of tension, to be targeted. There had been mosques burned in Western Herzegovina. There have been church towers dynamited in Central Bosnia before the last elections last year. There have been churches fired, also in Central Bosnia since. All these things that have happened, we have to be interested in. One of my duties as a UNESCO representative is to make sure that sacral buildings, sacral property are respected. Sadly enough, there are cycles, in which even in the peace time, they are not. Earlier this year, I was requested by ICTY to help them in terms of gathering information, evaluating information, that is, evaluating information that the Tribunal had, but also going out in the terrain to see what the situation was in the municipalities which are covered by this trial, the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak. So from April to June, this year, this is what I did. I examined mosques, mesjids and mektebs in these three municipalities, and the rest of my presentation will be more or less, a summary of this information I gathered and also the information which was made available to me here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go into that description, Dr. Kaiser, why is this important? Why you as a representative of UNESCO, why is this issue concerning the sacral and cultural monuments and the safeguarding of those monuments an important issue?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It's important for reasons that are sort of second nature to people, but often sometimes harder to spell out. People are attached to their environment, first of all. Secondly, they are attached to specific objects in their own environment. If you take a building like Vijecnica, the national university library in Sarajevo, people are not attached to it because they know the name of the architect or they admire it aesthetically. They are attached to it because they had rendezvoused with their girlfriends in front of. Maybe they spent many good hours reading books in it. It's a landmark. It's something that is part of their lives. Maybe as time goes on, they start to know a little bit more about it and what it represents, what it signifies, in terms of the history of the town or the history of their district. So in an unconscious way, people are very attached to their environment and the buildings in their environment. I'm talking about built cultural heritage, I'm not talking about manuscripts, et cetera, et cetera. Other buildings are closer perhaps to the cultural sole, the cultural psyche. You asked this question because, in the society which we leave, we are an extremely urbanised society and very often we will admire Notre Dame because we know what century Notre Dame was built in, we know something about its history, its aesthetics have been explained to us. We live in secularised societies. We don't always, immediately responsible, to the simple messages that is in a lot of the sacral heritage. But there are societies and there are populations in any society which are extremely attached to certain types of buildings. They are a symbol of their past. A church contains often a cemetery. A cemetery contains the graves of our ancestors. A church also were most important parts of your life have gone through. You may have been married in the church. You may be buried in the church. The church points upwards. Religious buildings, sacral buildings are very, very important for the cycle of life. When you have the society groups in the society for whom those things are really important, then if you touch the church, if you touch the mosque, then you are touching something very, very important to those people. As we are talking here basically about sacral buildings, I think that's basically my answer. This is an intangible thing, but an extremely important thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If those sacral buildings, let us stay with the sacral buildings, are destroyed or damaged, what effect might that have on the population, the particular ethnic population, when they see and observe such a destruction?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I think there's a sense of desolation, a sense of being especially wounded. I think the destruction of a mosque is different than the destruction of a Bosnian Muslim's house. The mosque or the church or whatever, it represents an order to the world. What happens to you, everybody knows that you're mortal. Your life is a series of accidents. But the mosque, the church, it represents an order. When you destroy that, you are sort of tempering, threatening the order of existence. I think that one reacts in that sense. It has often been said to me, during the war, and not just about churches, but about other major cultural buildings, that we get used to being killed. We know that human life is no more tangible or tougher than the life of a butterfly, but when we see these other buildings being destroyed, then the world starts to crumble around us. And I think it's more so, in the case of sacral buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to the actual destruction of the Islamic cultural and sacral buildings. If you can begin your discussion, Doctor, with a brief overview of what you're talking about vis-à-vis these buildings, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: To go back a little bit to the question you asked before, you asked it generally, but there's also a specific application in terms of the area that is being under concern. These municipalities are overwhelming rural.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Kiseljak and --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Kiseljak, Busovaca and Vitez. Kiseljak, which is the biggest town but it's a small sort of country town for us. Busovaca, Vitez, or Novi Travnik; these are very small places and they are surrounded by a sort of curia of villages. One thing that has to be kept in mind, in discussing the rural population, and we're talking specifically about the rural Bosniaks, is that this is something that very much impressed me in 1994 when I went there. When I went to Mostar in November 1992, there were these fabulous town mosques, stone mosques, but a lot of them were being used as galleries or museums. They were not being used for the cult. One of them, the Carados Begova (phoen) mosque was the frescos the very interesting fresco and it was being restored. So there was a big scaffolding inside, but this a process that was going to take years and years and years to carry out. When you went to the countryside, you found the plethora of mosques all over the place. And I was trying to identify cultural heritage, so I would have pictures from the 1920s or something of a mosque, and I would be sort of junketing around the countryside looking for this mosque, and I couldn't find this mosque. I couldn't find this mosque because it had been totally transformed by the imam, by the community over time. Everybody questioned their tastes, their tastes in colours, their tastes in objects, et cetera, et cetera, but there was no doubt about it that these mosques were alive and that they were important for the rural community. I had many examples of seeing people go to the mosque and a lot of people going to the mosque. There were a lot of new mosques in the countryside as well. A lot of these mosques were built or built partially with funds from the “gastarbeiter”, the emigrant workers who went to Germany, who went elsewhere. There was a kind of vitality in the countryside, and this was proof of a kind of devotion, a devoutness, on the country population. This is the general rule all over the world. If we wanted to look at Western Herzegovina, we wouldn't understand it either if we didn't understand the Franciscans and the role of the Catholic church in the lives of the people. It's the same thing in rural Bosnia, in as much as the Bosnian Muslims themselves are concerned. To talk about the types of buildings which are under consideration here, well, it's quite simple. We have mosques. A mosque has a minaret to distinguish it from a mesjid. It's often called Friday mosque. To give you an example of how important a mosque is in the local life, when I was in one village called Rotilj, I spoke to the head man of the village. This little village is sort of at the end of a valley, and the road out of the valley goes through Kiseljak. So there was a Bosnian Muslim population living in this village. They were going to the mekteb, using it as a mosque. He said to me, "I hope that after the war, the mosque in Kiseljak will be available to us so we can go there for Dzuma on Friday." So on Friday, and you see this all over the territory, it's market day. It's also Dzuma. So people will go from a whole series of little villages around the town, they will go to the mosque which has the minaret. They will go do their devotions there; they will meet their friends there; they will exchange a lot of news there. So this is another way of pointing out how important the mosque is for the community's life on, sort of, a wider level. A mosque is one type of building. In this area, there were very few minarets traditionally. There were little minarets that were built in the roof of the mosque. They only went up a few metres high. They rested on the beams in the ceiling. Later on, in the post-war period, a lot of minarets began to appear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about post-war, you're talking about World War II?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, World War II, yes. The other type of cult building, of course, is the mesjid, which is basically a mosque without a minaret. It's a type of small one-roomed orbit, several rooms sometimes because it's combined with other functions. It's a small building that you find in the countryside. The third type of building is the mekteb. The mekteb is a school for primary-school-aged children. This is for the study of the Koran. It's also where the children learn Arabic. Mekteb often serves as a mesjid, in fact, in the country area. A function that you find in modern religious buildings is the gasulhane which is for washing the dead. Now, traditionally, mosques and mesjids, they had that specific function. More and more recently, you find a building which will have all functions put into it, mekteb, mesjid or mosque, gasulhane. And you find a lot of older buildings have adapted to have a mekteb room for the teaching of the children and also for the gasulhane. One remark about the Islamic sacral and educational buildings from a historical point of view in this area, I think, should be made. The buildings here are not as striking as the great urban heritage or even some of the rural heritage. The mosques in the Vitez area have nothing in common, except for one, with the great mosque of Travnik which was just a few kilometres down the road. The mosques in the Kiseljak area haven't anything in common, of course, with the Sarajevo mosques. None the less, there are mosques of important. In Stari Vitez, there's the Ahmed Aga mosque built at the end of the 16th century. We will have a chance, I think, to see a picture of this later on. We have the Vares mosque from the 16th century in Busovaca. In Kazagici, which is north of Kiseljak, there is the old mosque which dates, I think, from the middle of the 16th century. There's an old mosque in Han Ploca. I'm not when it was built. It was rebuilt in 1960. There is a mosque in Bukve, north of Vitez, built at the end of the 19th century, and the mosque in Bukavica, which has an undetermined date. All of these are stone buildings, but they are not representative of all the types of buildings, sacral or educational Islamic buildings you find in the area. After World War II, a lot of brick buildings, and brick buildings often of quality, which were built. You will find mosques in Gromljak and Hercezi. There are a lot of mektebs. The mektebs are not very distinguishable, also it should be said, from private houses, which may have something to do with their survival. There are also here and there, not so many of them in this area, there are turbe. Turbes are tombs, and they are tombs, usually, of important historical figures, and they look like little tiny houses. So there are a few of these in the area as well. From the 1970s on, a lot of sacral buildings went up, and they are very poor quality. They are hollow block, cement minarets. There's a proliferation of minarets that date, actually, from the 1950s where brick minarets were added to a lot of buildings, and then, of course, a lot of mosques now which are built with minarets. I think it's something ironic in the sense that the minaret is a sign of Muslims living there, but before the war, say, in the last 30 years of the war, which is not considered to be a golden age of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are more signs of this on the horizon than there were before. Just before the war, there were lots of mosques and mektebs that were being built, and you will see a few of these in the photographs as well. Now, I think I should maybe say something about how one goes about finding buildings in the countryside, because this is important. If you don't have a reasonable sample of something, you can't draw conclusions from it from what you've seen from your sample. The major source for information that was given to ICTY was lists of Islamic sacral buildings in these municipalities. These lists are a little confusing because they don't differentiate between buildings. They just give a long list of functions. For example, in one place they will indicate there's a mesjib, a mekteb and a gasulhane, but you don't know if there is one building or it there is two buildings or even, eventually, three buildings. That makes it a little bit problematic when you are trying to look for them. Sometimes buildings on these lists are indicated as mesjids when, in fact, they are mektebs. This sort of exaggerates the importance of the building, but at the same time, it is an indication of the function of the building changed during the war where a mesjid, in fact, because the people -- or a mekteb, because people didn't have access to a mosque, the mekteb was used as a mosque for prayers. In these lists, there's sometimes a doubt also whether or not a building actually existed, and there are several cases where I'm not at all certain that there was a building there like that before the war. In a couple of cases, buildings were, in fact, forgotten. In this case where they were forgotten, they were not badly damaged buildings. Maybe that's why they were forgotten. Maybe they were forgotten because the dzemat which is sort of like a parish for the Islamic community, its boundaries don't necessarily correspond to the boundaries of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you please ask the witness to slow down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get that message, Doctor? If you can pause for a little bit. I believe we were going to move to the maps and we were going to give some indication of the areas that you studied and what you found. Those maps are with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, if we can give out those four sets of maps at first, and we start with those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 451.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can also give the witness 452 as well, the next map. I'm sorry, Mr. Dubuisson, it might be easier to give the other two out as well so the witness can go through them in series. I apologise. Mr. President and Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for reference purposes, the four maps, 451 through 454, are just cut-up versions of Exhibit 29. It's a little difficult to see for Your Honours and counsel when it's at the easel. So it's just easier, I thought, and more expeditious if Dr. Kaiser just explained it in a smaller format using the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can use those four exhibits, I believe we have them set up. The one on the easel at this juncture is Exhibit 451. Can you explain your work, obviously, exactly what you were attempting to accomplish? You might want to explain the colour scheme first.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, on the map that have you in front of you, you see only two colours, but on all the maps you will see four. Blue represents a building that is destroyed. It's destroyed because the load bearing construction system is so badly damaged that all you can do with this building is just to bulldoze it. The other colour that you will see, which you don't see on this first map, is orange. Orange means the building is very severely damaged in its construction system by explosives, or it means that a building has been totally burned out, no roof. All the internal fixtures, everything is gone. It is severely damaged. It can be repaired, but it often looks as if it's destroyed. Green means moderate damage, some damage to the roof structure, maybe an artillery impact in the wall, some burning, but the basic structural system is not affected. Yellow means light or no damage. The yellow mark indicates that a building could be used after, you know, a certain minimum amount of work. The other three colours imply that the building is not usable. The functions are, in fact, destroyed. Obviously, there are some cases that do not fit conveniently into any one of these four categories, and I'll point them out. I will explain what is on this first map. This first map contains buildings on the lists of the Islamic community in Armija-controlled areas. All together, there are 26 Islamic sacral and educational buildings on these first two maps. This first map is the Vitez and Busovaca municipality. I don't know if you can see everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could provide him with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I have the pointer here, but I think I have to move the map around. Okay, that's very good, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be helpful to turn the ELMO towards you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The first comment that can be made about this map, Vitez and Busovaca municipalities, is -- by the way, why are these buildings here? They were indicated on the lists of the Islamic community as being severely damaged or completely destroyed. In other words, I had to go and look at them in order to find out what had happened in the area. You can see from the first map that nearly all of them are indicated as lightly damaged or no damage. That was their condition. There are two exceptions. One of the exceptions is the building in Vitez. In Stari Vitez, this is the Ahmed Aga mosque. The other one is the mosque in Bukve. In both of these cases, I consider that the damage was probably moderate, but for one of them, Bukva mosque, it could have been lighter. One of the problems is that the buildings have often been repaired since the war. So it is very difficult. Nobody has photographs. People come and tell you what happened to it, and very often they exaggerate. Maybe we will pass to -- there's a picture of this mosque in Stari Vitez, but maybe we will pass to the other map first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever is easiest for you. The one on the ELMO right now is 451, and we can move to the next map which is 451. This has two areas of notation, Doctor, and we're going to ask the usher to move that onto the camera at some juncture because there are two different locales. Again, 452 is an area in around the Kiseljak area, and you have the two contrasting corners marked.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: At the top corner what you have is four buildings, and that represents sort of the front-line area. The Armija was in control of that area. Those buildings are all light or lightly damaged or not at all damaged. Then you have buildings down in the right-hand corner. The two green buildings, the two green indications, are mosques, Bukovica and Sokolic. In both of these cases, there is artillery damage to the mosques, but the direction of the impacts is from the east or south-east. It is highly unlikely that this damage was, in fact, done by HVO. The conclusions here are that the mosques which were, in fact, on the front-line in the Armija positions which could -- not all of these could easily be attained. Visibility on them was not always -- some of them were not so visible. But the conclusion here is that, in fact, there is very little damage. It's not the type of artillery damage which one is used to seeing on the mosques on the frontlines between the Armija and the BSA, a totally different situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you want to move to the next map at this juncture or would you prefer to move to the pictures?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I was thinking, perhaps, showing the mosque in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, if we can move to the series of photographs commencing with the first two photographs. Not those photographs, Mr. Usher, the ones that are in the binder. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 455.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're looking at 455/1.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is going to be, I think, the most idyllic picture of all of the selection here. This is a picture I took in June 1994 of the Ahmed Aga mosque in Stari Vitez. This is arguably the finest building in the whole area. The reason is that this stonework here is extremely, extremely fine, a very carefully crafted building. There is almost no other building that you can actually see such stonework in the whole area. The minaret was added later. There is a graveyard around it, and you can see from this, it looks fairly untouched. The damage on this mosque, on this mosque here, is, in fact, what would permit you to classify it as light. You will see there's two piercing impacts in the minaret, but they don't damage the stability of the minaret. On the surface of the mosque, you can see a sort of diagonal line of small arms fire. But if you look at the roof, you see something has been done to the roof. We have another picture which explains why this would be considered to be moderately damaged. This picture, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This photograph, Mr. President and Your Honours, was taken by then Lieutenant Michael Duly of the British battalion during the Cheshire's tour in April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is interesting because you see the addition, the front addition gasulhana and mekteb on the right-hand side, but you see something in the roof which is extremely interesting. If you look at the rows of tiles on the roof, you see that they are all sort of -- they are out of whack, I would say, but they are not properly aligned. There's an awful lot of tiles on the south-eastern side which have fallen off. Now, what is this? I think this is the result of the truck bomb in Stari Vitez. These home-made, crude weapons often had very considerable destructive power. The truck bomb in Mostar set off, in fact, a small earthquake. In the gymnasium in Mostar, which I went over with an engineer, it was pointed out to me that it looked like the building had gone through an earthquake. What happened with this building in Stari Vitez was that when the bomb went off, the roof rose and then fell back, which explains this movement of the tiles. Not only do you have to replace the tiles, but you also have to look at the roof structure itself, because probably the wooden structure was also damaged. So this explains why this would be considered to be a moderately damaged building. That's all for this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we're moving back to the map arrangement, and if we could move to the next map, which is 353, Dr. Kaiser, with the assistance of the usher. These next two maps, can you just start off with what that represents before you begin your explanation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This map represents the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca, and here you can see there are three -- this is HVO-controlled territory. You can see here that there are different colours. There's only one green or moderately damaged, Donji Vecerska. However, on this particular map, there are three blues, which means three destroyed buildings, and there are four buildings which are severely damaged. This is the first part of the other map. You can take all the buildings together that were seen or for which photographic evidence was seen in the three municipalities, you find that these two maps, they contain 26 Islamic sacral and educational buildings under HVO control. Three of them are in the municipality of Busovaca. There are five in Vitez municipality, and there are 18 in Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just turn to that next map, we have 453 on the ELMO. Just for the record, I know you discussed the next map, which is 454, that represents the Kiseljak area under HVO control and the various destruction that took place in the Kiseljak area; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct. This map has another colour which is the colour yellow. You will see here that there is only one blue marking, Hercezi. There is, however, a larger number of orange. There are three moderately damaged buildings, and then there are a whole collection of yellows, which are lightly damaged or not all damaged. As you can see from this, most of those are south and south-east of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's worthwhile sort of recapitulating, first of all, what is on the maps. There's 26 buildings here. Of these 26, over half, that is 14, are severely damaged or destroyed. That's 54 per cent. If you add the moderately damaged buildings, you get 18, and that makes 69 per cent of the buildings seen or for which there is photographic evidence. In the Vitez and Busovaca municipalities, all damaged sacral buildings are in the moderate to destroyed category. In Kiseljak, 10, or 55 per cent in the moderate to destroyed categories with, again, as I said, the least damage category being south of the Kizeljak area. There are pictures now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to recapitulate again, between these three municipalities, among these three municipalities, the ones that are severely damaged and destroyed or moderately damaged or worse is 69 per cent?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the individual photographs, Mr. Usher, and the photographs we are going to start with will be the photographs that are part of Exhibit 47/1, which is the photographs to Dr. Kaiser's right that have been received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just to recapitulate, the yellow is lightly damaged?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is, or not damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or not damaged. The green?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The green is moderately damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Moderately. And the blue?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The blue is destroyed. Orange is severely damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can flip those over, Mr. Usher, we are going to start with 47/1, which is the photograph of the Ahmici mosque, the lower mosque. You have to take it out, yes.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that there are four buildings destroyed amongst this whole group of 26. They are destroyed, all of them, by explosives. One of them, there's a bit of doubt if it's severely damaged or destroyed, but we will get to that one. This is the Ahmici mosque, recently built, as I say, out of this cement block structure. This building is destroyed. The minaret looks as if -- it's possible it was mined in two places, one of them being just below the second sharafe and perhaps at the base of the minaret. This is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. This sharafe, can you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The sharafe is the gallery. In the modern mosques, the minarets sometimes have two galleries where the muezzin goes up, and traditionally he would call the faithful from the gallery or the sharafe. This is an expert job. The minaret has been brought down on top of the roof. So the artifices don't simply have a lot of explosives. They know exactly where to put them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next photograph, which is 47/30. No, that's not the photograph, sir. The photograph is one of the upper mosque, photograph 47/30. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, this is the mesjid in Ahmici. There's a better one than this one, in fact, a better photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it's 47/31, which is the one right below it. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, is the one that you're putting on 47/31?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move to 47/31, I believe that's the photograph you were discussing, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, this is simply more graphic. There have been several charges placed in this building. You can look at these corner posts here, the reinforcing structure here. Everything has been blown out. It's well-placed, but it's a bit obvious that this building is really finished. There's nothing you can do except bulldoze this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, just by way of clarification, the mosque that you noted in 47/1 in Ahmici, that is a traditional mosque with a minaret?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an example, is it not, of a mesjid, a mosque without a minaret?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, this was destroyed through a charge of some fashion?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Several charges. Maybe they're tank mines. Tank mines are commonly used to knock out houses and other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photograph, Mr. Usher. It is in the series here, and I believe that will then be photograph 455/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, Doctor, that is the next photograph in your series. Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the mesjid at Skradno. On the left-hand side, you can see the gasulhana here with a slab to wash the dead. There are two stories here, and then there's -- there were two stories here, and then there was a roof on top of it. The explosives have been used here. They have brought down the upper story. They have knocked out the structure in this part of the building, and they have brought the ceiling down on it. I think the next picture is also very interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 455/4, again, another photograph of the Skradno mesjid?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: You can see the ceiling. If you look to the right, you can see the type of damage done to the walls which are leaning in. You can see other types of cracks which are extremely telltale about what the situation of the building is. This building, which is also like the other preceding two, same sort of structures, same type of materials, this building is destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next mosque, I believe, is the Hercezi mosque, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By way of reference, if we can just look at Exhibit 68/1 and 2, and just have you take a look at those and identify those as the same mosque that you will then discuss in 455/5. Doctor, that is Exhibit 68/1. That is the Hercezi mosque, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: On the left, there is the Hercezi mosque, and in the middle is the Hercezi mekteb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point with your pointer to those two facilities distinguishing between the mosque and the mekteb?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the mosque here, and this is the mekteb right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. At this point, if we could now move to the photograph in your series 455/5, which I believe is yet another angle of the Hercezi mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you could put that on the ELMO, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, in fact, another angle of the Hercezi mosque, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The lens in this camera is a little bit distorting. That's the only problem with this picture. What has happened here is that the minaret has been mined, and this has done a lot of damage to the front of the mosque. In the preceding picture on the opposite wall, through the windows, there is other damage which has been done from the explosion. I think that this building is destroyed, that you cannot save it. You can't see them so well. There are other cracks which are indicative here of the damage that has been done. Some people might argue that you could, in fact, save this building, but it's in very, very bad condition. It should be kept in mind that this is also the similar type of building materials, and these hollow block buildings, cement structures, are very easy, in fact, to knock out. I should perhaps say that this dubious -- this case which is discussible, it's in the Kiseljak area. The preceding three are in Vitez and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, again, is another one that had some type of charge placed to it?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, in the minaret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this juncture, we are moving from the various conditions of mosques to those that were severely damaged, are we not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you continue with that explanation, sir, beginning with the first photograph, which is 455/6?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, now we are moving towards buildings that are severely damaged. This means that they can be rebuilt, but it also means that they are totally out of function and there is a certain amount of expense to do so. This first building is the recently built mosque in Grbavica in Vitez. This is a picture I took in June 1994. You can see that this building has no roof here. That's where the roof should be, of course. There was a roof there, but that roof has probably been burned or dismantled. More importantly, right in the middle you see where the minaret was surrounded by rubble, which comes from the charge that was placed in the minaret. You can see the type of damage which has been done by the explosion here, to the post here, here, and even here as well. This is the first example of a severely damaged mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The roof of this structure was burned, was it not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: From this picture, you cannot -- it looks like there's some traces of black here, which means that the fire would be inside. The roof is gone. I mean, I'm not sure if it was burned or not. I didn't climb up onto it to see, but it's gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next building that we're talking about is the Vares mosque in 455/7. Before we do that, if we could just look at the outside of that structure that is depicted in photograph 60/1, if we could. The Vares mosque is the mosque that is in downtown Busovaca, is it not, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Vares mosque from the exterior, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This also gives you a better understanding of why I was very confused when I was going around in 1994 because this is a recent structure, a gasulhana and mekteb which has been added to the front of the historic mosque. This picture shows burning damage in the structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to your photograph 455/7.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is a photograph I took in June 1994 of the interior of the mosque. You can see where it has been burned. Also, of cultural interest, this mosque didn't have a minaret. It had a minaret on the side. It had a minaret in the roof, and the minaret would have rested on beams which you see that have been burned there. This is, in fact, a stone mosque. This is a 16th century mosque. This is a building of great value, even though it has been changed. You can see the rendering which is peeling off. Almost no where can you see the stones. As bad as this looks, and this mosque is severely damaged, this mosque can be rebuilt using the original structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next structure which is the Lancari mesjid, which is depicted in 455/8?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I'm a little sorry about the quality of this picture, because the interior, you can't see it so well. This is a case, also, of a building which -- I think it's in very, very tricky condition. Now, I'll explain the charge - there seems to have been one charge - was placed inside on the ceiling where it made a hole. You can't see it here in this reproduction, but there is -- here, there are a series of structures like this, these cross-beams, concrete beams, and the whole interior wall of block is blown out. This wall is blown out. Then this wall has actually been moved, you see?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Over on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, on the left-hand side. This has actually been moved. This is in an extremely dangerous condition. This building, if you leave it this way, it means the whole distribution of weight on the building corner has changed. So it is all leaning. If it isn't given attention, it is going to be in trouble. You can also argue that this is moderately damaged. I mean, if you take pictures of this building from the other sides, you don't see this damage, but this is serious damage done by explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move to the next photograph which is the Gacica mekteb which is 455/9 in that series. If we could also give Dr. Kaiser the next photograph which is also part of the series, 455/10, for ease of moving the photographs on and off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Like the preceding building, the Lancari building, it has the mesjid, mekteb and gasulhana. You could see that it was unfinished. This in Gacica is a mekteb and gasulhana. It was, in fact, being used before the war, apparently, but, in fact, it is rather in an unfinished condition. This is also of the interior. I'm afraid that what you're looking at in the corner is the remains of the internal rendering, and you can see at the top -- you can see where it is burned. I mean, yes, this building has been completely burned out. There is no wood left here either, I'm afraid. It's severely damaged, but if you put the roof back on and put the rendering on, you can actually put it back into function. I should say that the number of severely damaged buildings is ten, and we have just seen four of them which are from the Vitez and the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we are now moving to the Kiseljak area to discuss the mosque first in Gromljak; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we first just cross-reference the photographs that are in evidence and first look at Exhibit 67 in evidence, 1 and 2. Let's just take a quick glance at these photographs in evidence, Doctor, beginning with Exhibit 67/1. Is that an exterior shot of the Gromljak --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I guess it's the Gromljak mekteb --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mosque, I'm sorry. The next photograph, 67/2, is that a photograph of the interior of the Gromljak mosque?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the next photograph in your series, 455/11. If we could pan that back just a bit, thank you. Doctor, can you explain the damage to this facility?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the Gromljak mosque. This is a brick mosque, and actually this is a rather nice building, built, I think, after World War II. An explosive charge has been placed in the minaret and has done considerable damage. Besides destroying the minaret, the brick has fallen all over the place and has helped to break up the roof. There is considerable damage which has been done to the entrance part of the mosque. This is bad damage - it is severely damaged - but brick structures are often far more resilient and can be put back together far more easily than they look. This building is probably recoupable. One of the problems, though, is that if people do come back to this area and they look at it, the problem is that they will probably knock it down, not try to reconstruct it, and will build a new one with a concrete minaret and the hollow block walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, if we could move to the next mosque, which is the Visnjica mosque, and if we could first reference photographs in evidence 73/1 and 73/2. 73/1, which is on the ELMO, that is, in fact, an angle shot of the Visnjica mosque, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, 73/2, that is a shot of the interior, is it not, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, that's the interior. It is looking directly towards the mihrab or the prayer niche right here. It is an interesting photograph because it also gives us a certain idea of the toughness of the building as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move to your series of photographs 455/12 and 13, we have two angle shots of the Visnjica mosque. If you could use them in your explanation of the damage to this building.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The Visnjica mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the similar type of damage that's done to Gromljak. The charge has been placed in the minaret here. It's blown in the wall. It has probably also helped bring down part of the roof. The building is severely damaged, but probably recoupable.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: More or less the same view with a slightly different angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps this would the time to take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That would be fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is now resumed. Have the accused brought in, please? The accused, please? We seem to have lost the Defence attorney and I hope we haven't lost the accused also. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, we were staying in the Kiseljak municipality and discussing severely damaged mosques, mesjids, mektebs and turbe and we were talking about Visnjica, and now we want to move to the Kiseljak mosque, and for that purpose, Mr. President, Your Honours, we will look at Exhibits 63/1, 63/2 and 63/3. Dr. Kaiser?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the mosque in Kiseljak. It shows the mosque from the other side of the road. The minaret has been dynamited. This is a brick mosque, by the way. The dome looks as if it's been stripped of some of the lead covering. This is, I think, rather an expert job. The artifices could have put the mosque, minaret down on top of the building. And it seems like a few bricks right here, but most of it is right beside the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move to the interior shots and just go to 63/2, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think what's interesting about this is it shows some burning damage in the entrance part of the mosque here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to that, please?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, all of this here. You can see the black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the black areas on the ceiling as well as on the sides?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last photograph on the Kiseljak mosque is 63/3?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This also shows some burning damage, I think, here. There's also rubble as well. This is not a very good photograph, but the mihrab here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The mihrab is the place that's pointing towards Mecca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's right. This looks as if it's been vandalised. It's hard to tell from the photograph. But it is interesting that in some cases, it seems that the fire was lit right in the mihrab or right in front of the mihrab, and in this case, it looks like some damage done to the structure to the mihrab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some burnt damage, as well, on the walls?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can move to the next mosque and is the Han Ploca mosque, and if we can, just for reference purposes, put Exhibit 398 on the ELMO before we move to the next exhibit. That is the Han Ploca mosque, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your series of photographs, let's look at 455/14 which is just a different angle of that Han Ploca mosque. That is obviously a different time of year photograph, Doctor, but nonetheless, is that not the Han Ploca mosque?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Han Ploca mosque. You can see the old structure, this sort of rubble stone structure behind here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the top of the building now?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Here, right here. This is the front of the old mosque right here. That's the old mosque structure there and then this is the newer, the brick structure, gasulhane and mekteb, I believe in here. This damage looks like burning damage, except in the front, there may have been an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph is 455/15, which is the Gomionica mekteb.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, this photo dates from this year. It was during the tour that I took of the area. Gomionica mekteb has been completely burnt out. You can tell there's still a burnt beam at the top here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are pointing to the top of the photograph, the top of the building where you can see that burnt beam; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the Gomionica mekteb; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the mekteb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, 455/16 in the series there, thank you. Doctor, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is an interesting structure. This is a turbe. This is another -- inside of this, on the top of the floor is a catafalque and underneath, in the ground, should be buried the body of a notable. I have information that this, in fact, is the turbe of Sejh Ismail Harisani who was the commander of the Sultans army in the 15th century. This is not information that comes from -- it doesn't come from a cultural heritage institute, so I take it with a grain of salt, but it should be pointed out that these turbe, in the countryside, usually turn out to be important people from the past. The form of this building, this is not an original, old building. This was made in the'70s or '80s, something like that. It looks from this photograph as if it were burned, but there could be burning damage at the top here, but it's not entirely conclusive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noted that you had heard from sources that this was the tomb of a commander of the Sultan's army from the 15th century?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It's a written source which is -- it's from an official source, not a cultural source. I think it's a ministry -- the ministry of the interior. It is interesting that this -- a turbe, a historic turbe figures on lists of cultural heritage from the cultural heritage institutes that they do not identify who is in it. So, this a little problematic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people in the area believe that that was a turbe in which a significant Islamic leader was buried?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's different. I don't know what the people in the area believed, but these objects, they attach -- they have that kind of importance, and they regard it that way. Whether or not X is X or X is Y who is buried there, the local people think it's somebody. Yes, I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recapitulate on these buildings in the Kiseljak municipality that you just discussed, before we move on?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay. There were six buildings that were severely damaged in the Kiseljak area, compared to four in Busovaca and Vitez. These severely damaged buildings in four cases it's been explosives, in four of the cases it's been fire, in two cases, maybe more, it's a combination of firing and also explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're going to move into an area, Doctor, of Islamic, sacral buildings that received less damage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we start with the first photograph, 455/17, and if we could place that on the ELMO and if you could identify that, Doctor, and begin to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I recall that there are four buildings in these three municipalities, in this situation. This building is the Donji Vecerska mekteb. It's in the Vitez municipality. This building has been pillaged. The roof has been stripped. All the black of the roof structure, there is a little bit -- well, it's a bit misleading, at least from what I can see on my screen. There was a burning attempt made on the roof, very circumscribed, but basically this is a stripping, pillaging operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, which is 455 -- excuse me -- 455/18, if we could put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the unfinished mosque at Duhri. There appears to have been an explosion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the centre of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The centre of the photograph. There's not much rubble from this explosion. I've seen written sources, official sources, that claim that the minaret was dynamited. It's highly possible the minaret was not finished, but the damage is from explosives, and this is moderate damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was, in fact, another building that you mentioned in a prior photograph which had moderate damage, and that was the Hercezi mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for reference purposes, if we could just take a quick look at that --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Excuse me, mekteb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could take a quick look at 68/1, I believe that we could go back and reference that particular mosque, that particular mekteb, excuse me. It's this photograph, Mr. Usher. This one. I know this is some degree of repetition, here, Doctor, but, again, the mosque is on the left and the mekteb is the centre building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just point to that for the record, the centre building in white. Can you tell us about that damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I can only Judge from the photograph because I haven't seen the building -- I say moderately damaged because the roof is clearly gone completely. You look in the upper story windows, you don't see any signs of daylight. It looks as if the ceiling is a concrete ceiling. The inside may have burned, may not have burned. The roof may have burned -- the roof construction may have been stripped, but this is a moderately damaged building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photograph which is 66/1 and 2, it's the Jehovac mesjid, the Svinjarevo mesjid. Continue, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the Jehovac mesjid which suffered pillaging, burning, some stripping of the roof as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go to that next photograph? Is that the inside of that Jehovac mesjid?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This is the inside. This is probably -- well, it's hard to say from this photograph, it's not very good, but photographs I took of it after this showed that there had been a burning attempt made on the mosque, but it didn't do substantial damage, I don't think, to it. You can see that this internal roof structure is still intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, were there any other buildings in the Kiseljak municipality that suffered some light damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, in fact, there are eight buildings in this category, suffering the light damage. One case of light damage is simply a broken window. On all but one of these buildings were mektebs, and there's one picture of a mekteb that has light damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go to that photograph? That would be 455/19.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: All right. This is the mekteb and gasulhane in Gornji Palez. You can on the roof, damage from small arms. But what is down here looks to me like stripping. One thing that has to be kept in mind is that sometimes buildings -- well, considering the amount of damage done to roof tiles during the war, people would go and they would take tiles off the roof. This is interesting because this seemed only have to remove roof tiles on the part of the roof that is over -- that overhangs the building, is the kind of consideration given to the building. The building also seems to have been pillaged inside. You couldn't approach it because there was a problem with mines in this area, but this is the typical kind of light damage. It doesn't take too much to get that building repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher, I think we are through with all our photographs at this point. As we move ahead, Doctor, can we move to the subject of certain information you received concerning this destruction, and if you could carry on with that portion of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay. To be very honest, I received very little information about the exact dates of destruction of buildings during my touring around about Grbavica mosque 1994. I was told by ECMM that it was burned in April 1993. I had a discussion with a Croatian refugee child, at the site of Grbavica, who told me that the mosque had been mined two weeks before in the month of May, around the 20th of May, 1994. The Vares mosque, the ECMM told me that it was burned possibly in September 1993 and that the minaret was mined in March 1994. In Jelinek mesjid which was in Armija territory, there was an attack on the village, and a Bosniak villager from the village explained to me that this took place on the 17th of April, 1993. Skradno mosque, Bosniak returnees told me that it was mined during an HVO attack in October 1993. Gomionica turbe, Bosniak returnee with whom I was speaking in June explained that it was burned in April 1998. I have been shown video evidence that shows that the catafalque was damaged before March or May 1996 when the film was taken. That is all the information I have about dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Let's turn to the subject of some general remarks you may want to tell the Trial Chamber about the destruction of Islamic and sacral and educational buildings in the HVO controlled areas. Could you do that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I think everything is sort of relative, and when you have had a lot of experience in the area, you tend to compare things that have happened in one area with things that you have seen in other areas. One first remark is that, as you remember from the first two maps, very, very little damage was done from HVO positions against mosques that were in Armija-controlled territory. There was extremely light damage. I don't know why. I don't know if it was a question of ordinance, I don't know if it was a question of will. But certainly compared to what the Bosnian Serbian artillery did to mosques, it's very, very negligible. My second comment is that there is no bulldozing of mosques or mesjids or mektebs in this area. Now, bulldozing is especially an urban phenomena. It seems to reflect more of a logical approach, more of a reasoned out approach to what one is doing. There are a lot of bulldozed mosques in Republic Srpska, not just in towns, but also in villages. There's one bulldozed mosque in Mostar west, the Balinovac mosque. There are no bulldozed mosques in Vitez, Busovaca or Kiseljak municipalities, and it's interesting, the Kiseljak mosque, that could have been a candidate for bulldozing, if somebody wanted to do it. As I pointed out, even the mining of the mosque is a bit odd. They knocked down the minaret. I've been in some places where a building was damaged and later on authorities used the damage to it as an excuse, they said, this building is dangerous, and they would then destroy the building. In the case of the mosque in Kiseljak, I suppose if you stand in the aperture where the bricks are, where the minaret was blown out, that's dangerous. But it doesn't present that degree of danger. You couldn't justify destroying it because it was a dangerous building. It could have been blown in such a way as to make the invocation of the danger the reason to destroy it, but it wasn't. So those are two beginning remarks. If you look at the three different municipalities in the HVO-controlled areas, you see that there is a difference. Of course, there are fewer Islamic and sacral and educational buildings in Vitez and Busovaca, but they are significantly more damaged than the sacral and educational buildings in the Kiseljak municipality. In Kiseljak, especially what seems to have survived are the mektebs. As I pointed out, the mektebs, they are somewhat more anonymous buildings. They very, very often look like houses. It's hard to find them because they don't stand out. Local people would have known where they were. If they were local people destroying, they would know exactly where to go, but in Kiseljak municipality, there was less damage, including even the major structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your analysis, there's more damage in Vitez and Busovaca than in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: There's more serious damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serious damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, more serious damage, yes. However, in both areas, it is to be said that both mosques and mesjids are damaged, badly damaged and should be recalled that there is not one minaret in HVO controlled territory. There's the minaret in Stari Vitez but there are no other minarets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you move on to the next point, you said there are no minarets standing in HVO-controlled territory, but the minaret is standing in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It was not HVO-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. Had that particular minaret been fired upon?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It had been fired upon, but not with great determination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: To recapitulate, one could say in the HVO-controlled territory, 54 per cent of the buildings were severely damaged or destroyed and 69 per cent showed moderate damage up to the level of total destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, based on your analysis and your work in the area, what significance do you attach to this destruction and damage to Islamic sacral buildings?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, the first obvious thing is that you are depriving local Muslims of a place of worship. I think that's the fairly obvious thing. Where there are minarets, there are Muslims. Where there are no minarets, it seems to say that there are no Muslims. I mean, this is remodelling the landscape to make it correspond to what the ethnic or national components of the landscape, in fact, are. Remove the minaret is a way of saying, "There are no Muslims here." I think we go back to the question of what the sacral building represents, especially for the rural population. I think this is a particularly strong, enduring injury inflicted upon the Bosniaks by this destruction. Given how important it is for them, this is close to sacrilege. It is a very strong way of saying to the Bosniak Muslims that, "We don't want to live with you anymore." There are a few other remarks that I think are in order as well. If you are going after an old building -- now, the old mosque in Stari Vitez, of course, is standing. There's a tradition about that mosque that the stone comes from a Roman bridge, that it was not cut for the mosque, it was in a Roman bridge. If you destroy this mosque, you are doing several different things.
