One of them is that you are sort of removing the memory -- it's been there since the end of the 16th century, you are removing the Muslims, not from just the present landscape or the future landscape, you are removing them from the past. In this case, you are even going back further. You are going to damage the perception of the past that everybody has had. If it goes far enough, you are taking the Muslims completely out of a chronology, not just out of space. You're saying that the Muslims were never there. Now, there's another question which is a very important question. I've thought about it a lot. It's common to regard the destruction of somebody else's cultural heritage as an attack on the other person. It is true. It is obvious. But it is more complicated than that. It is not just physically cleaning the society, removing the others, it also means changing the identity of one's own people. I think that we all have to take this much more into consideration now. What you're doing to the Croat from this area, is you're taking the Bosniak Muslim out of him. You are creating a new Croat. You are creating a Croat who has not the memory and the experience of having lived with somebody else. This is one of these -- I hope the last gasp of the 20th century of creating new men all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, when you were going through these areas, did you see a difference between the destruction of sacral monuments, and by sacral monuments, I say of all religious confessions, between areas controlled by the HVO and areas controlled by the Armija?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: In 1994, we were trying to get a complete picture of the damage to cultural and sacral buildings, because we were trying to be fair. We wanted to get the full range of destruction. As my trip in 1994, of the area, was not exhaustive, which means that I didn't see all of the mosques and all the mesjids. At the same time, we tried to see Serbian Orthodox churches and Catholic churches, and I did see some. I would say that the damage that was done in HVO-controlled territory to Bosniak sacral heritage was far greater intensity than the damage I saw carried out on Catholic churches outside the HVO-controlled territory. I could also point out that in Busovaca there was a late 18th century Orthodox church. I visited that church. Some local lady had a key. We went into it. It was perfectly intact in Busovaca, under HVO control. Outside the HVO-controlled territory, what did I see? I saw in Kacuni, I saw a recent church. This church was roughed up. It was pillaged, probably, I can't remember exactly, glass was broken in it. It was not burned. No burning attempt was made. I saw Guca Gora monastery. I was one of the first, I think, internationals allowed close to Guca Gora. I was not allowed into the monastery, that is either the church or the monastery buildings. I was told, either by ECMM or Armija or the Travnik authorities that the Armija had thrown out the mujahedeen after the mujahedeen had occupied it for two weeks. The building from the exterior, everything seemed okay. I have a cultural heritage assistant who, a few weeks ago, because we put Guca Gora on the list of national monuments in Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent my cultural heritage assistant to look at the church. Inside of it, there was graffiti from Armija elements. I visited the churches in Travnik. At the time of my mission, I believe that the Catholic church was actually functioning. It was not damaged by the local population. The Serbian Orthodox church was a little damaged to the exterior, perhaps, in fact, from bombardment from the BSA. It was closed up. There seemed to be no attempt to disturb the church. I visited a church in Dolac, which is just outside the western part of the Vitez pocket, a Catholic church, fine late 19th century building, which had some sort of military damage, I think, to the roof. Inside, it had been roughed up. It had been vandalised. There was some broken windows, but there was no attempt to burn. So what I would say is from the limited sample of buildings that I saw in the area, close to the frontlines, to the HVO positions, could even be seen by the HVO, in fact, there was much less damage done than to the Bosniak -- the Islamic sacral buildings inside of the Kiseljak and Vitez pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area that you visited in Kiseljak, Vitez, and Busovaca, you noted various buildings that had received dynamite charges, some very professionally done, according to your testimony, especially in Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, there are a few cases here. I mean the Ahmici mosque and the Kiseljak mosques, were very professional mosques, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything like that with the Orthodox and Catholic churches that you observed?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, outside of the HVO-controlled areas, I had not seen any mined buildings in those areas or even burned buildings. There are two burned Serbian Orthodox churches in the Bosna valley, south of the Lasva valley, those exist. Some of the Zepce pocket, I know of a village which has a Catholic church and that was burned. The ECMM said it was burned by the Armija. But this is far away from this area and is burning. What I say around the area was not very significant damage, compared to what we saw inside of the pockets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned in your testimony, several moments ago, that a destruction of a mosque and a minaret is sending a message to the Muslims that we do not want to live with you anymore; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be interpreted that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that activity, the destruction of these sacral monuments and sacral buildings be consistent with an attempt to remove the Muslim population from the area?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It would be consistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to responsibility, Doctor, and talk a little bit, if you will, based on your experience and your work in the area, of the responsibility of protecting these types of -- the cultural heritage and the sacral buildings in the former Yugoslavia, and specifically, Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, generally, this is kind of an obsessional question with us, from the international community, that's been involved with trying to do something with the cultural heritage during the war and afterwards. We often feel, first of all, we have an international responsibility that we did not exercise as much as we should have done. But let's get to sort of more operational and, perhaps, meaningful responsibilities in all countries. Civil authorities have a responsibility for protecting public property and cultural heritage which is listed by their services. The same thing, of course, is true in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The civil authorities had the responsibility in peace time, and at other times, to protect buildings that were listed. In Central Bosnia, in these HVO-controlled areas, the Vares mosque was listed as a third category monument, that is to say, a regional monument, sort of local importance. This was indicated in the materials provided by the institute to preserve cultural and historical and natural heritage of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also believe that probably the Ahmedija mosque was also a listed monument, but I haven't found any material to prove it, so far, in lists. At any rate, the civil authorities of Busovaca were obliged, they were -- they had a legal responsibility to protect the Vares mosque, and the Vares mosque was burned and the minaret was dynamited. There's another level of responsibility which is, of course, the responsibility of military authorities. Yugoslavia was a state's party to The Hague convention of 1954, on the protection of cultural heritage. It had a reputation, at least in UNESCO, of being a very good pupil of the convention, which is to say that it did inventories of cultural heritage of buildings which should be spared in case of war on its own territory. The Yugoslav armed forces were, apparently, taught well about cultural heritage, and the responsibilities they had to it. I remember at the beginning of war in Dubrovnik, The Hague convention flag came out all over the place. And I have seen over the years, many, many pictures of The Hague convention flag in Croatia especially, but also at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some countries refused to sign the convention. I believe that France refuses to fly this flag, and maybe for a good reason. Some people say this flag, in fact, attracts attention. In other words, the military had a responsibility to protect certain buildings, and this would include, at least, also the Vares mosque as a listed building. In the end, who exercised their responsibilities to protect these buildings? We've seen the pictures of these buildings. The buildings are badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would your consensus be that in the areas that you discussed and viewed in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, the HVO failed in that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have one moment to talk with my colleague, Mr. Harmon. Mr. President, I have no further questions of the Doctor at this point. I appreciate it. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All of these exhibits are going to be tendered as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Mr. President, that would be 451 through 455 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Hayman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kaiser. My name is Russell Hayman and I represent General Blaskic in these proceedings. You have a history degree, I take it?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the subject of your Ph.D. dissertation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The Masters of Request in Age of Descent of Centralisation of 1589 to 1660, I believe. That was the title of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What geographic area did that deal with?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That was France, old regime France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear it. I would have liked to know what was the title of the thesis. I got the date but I didn't get the title Could we hear it again, please?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The Masters of Request for Centralisation from 1589 to 1660.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did the interpreter get it? Very well, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside of your reports to and for the council of Europe, have you authored any publications on the subject matter of your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I have not published anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say, on direct, that you have previously testified before this court?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What case was that?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The ruling 61 regarding Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the month or date?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it is July of two years ago, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described your first mission to the Neretva valley and said that there were reprisals in response to conduct by the VRS or Bosnian Serb army. Who engaged in those reprisals, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I was guided by two Croats around all of these sites, and after hesitation on their part, they said, "Our side did it." To go into any greater detail, they didn't, and it would be -- I would say the people were specialists who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The persons who were touring you around, were they military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No, they were civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being toured around the Lasva and Kiseljak valleys, were there any admissions or confessions of guilt of responsibility by any tour guides or other persons, concerning destruction to Muslim cultural sites in those regions?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: My tour guides were the European community monitoring mission, that is, to say, mainly military people who had been in this area for a certain time and worked in it. The information came from them. There was no information coming from local people or opinions about who destroyed what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no such contacts, is that correct, on that trip?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Not with local people. I had contacts with -- I spoke with an Imam in Kacuni who accused the HVO. There were vague local -- there was the local standby person who said, "Oh, this was done by the HVO," that sort of comment which was made. This was usually about, you know, small arms fires or projectiles or some sort like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nothing specific and no details were passed to you by those types of --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No, nothing really detailed, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the May 1993 destruction of a mosque in Banja Luka. Do you know who may have been involved in that act or acts?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, referring to the destruction of, first of all, the Ferhadija mosque which is one of the finest mosques in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was, and the Arnodija (phoen) mosque in May, which promptly gave rise to a whole series of other incidents. These were all expert jobs. I don't know who destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who controlled the territory?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The Republic Srpska -- the Srpska territory, so it was controlled by the Serbian authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that your first visit to the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys was between the 30th of May and the 22nd of June, 1994?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was some two months after the signing of the Washington Agreement and the general crease fire in that region; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have obviously undertaken a study and provided the court with the statistical results, as well as, other testimony concerning your study. You said that you have received certain information here at the Tribunal. Can you explain what information, in your study, that is the basis of your testimony, came from your own inspection and what information have you summarised that was given to you here, at the Tribunal for the first time?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think I indicated that there are 52 buildings in this area, the 26 in the Armija-controlled area, and then there are 26 in the HVO-controlled areas. I visited about 24 of the buildings in the Armija-controlled area, and there are photographs that I took of most of those buildings. I visited and stopped -- let's put it this way, stopped at 16 of the buildings, got out, took photographs in the HVO-controlled areas, but many of the buildings, in fact, are on a main road, and they are evident. For example, Han Ploca mosque is on the main road, and I didn't take photographs. The photographs were taken earlier and submitted to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, with respect to, ten out of the 26 sites in HVO territory, you did not visit them on your tour, but you have been provided information and photographs here at the Tribunal which you've used and incorporated into your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think there's about half a dozen of them which I did not drive by and relied on photos completely, in my evaluation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photos provided to you after you arrived here at the Tribunal and prepared your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Before, before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photos -- let me correct that then. These photos that you described were provided to you by the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor in advance of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you incorporated that information in your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did you get the list of 52 buildings which formed the universe for your study?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The list was given to me by the Tribunal earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: By an individual or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it by a representative of the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that represented to you to be a comprehensive list of cultural sites in the area?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It was a translation, two versions. There is a translated version. There's a Serbo-Croatian version. It was represented to be what the Islamic community believed to be its sacral and educational property in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who, in the Islamic community, or what representative of the Islamic community, gave the list to the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they represent to you whether it had come from the interior ministry or the Bosnian intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It may have been. I really don't know. It may have been submitted through the interior ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not ask?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I would say this: I've seen so many lists in my profession, dealing with cultural heritage, I wasn't particularly interested in how it came through. I was more interested what was on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you were told to conduct a study or asked to conduct a study based on the universe of 52 buildings that had been selected by some other party who, as of right now, is not identified for the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: It's not 52 buildings. The way the list is broken down, it is broken down by function. As I said, one of the problems using the lists earlier, in an area, you would have place --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you could slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, first I would ask you to slow down. When you answer, please look to the Judges because you are answering for the Judges. You hear the question, you listen to the question, turn to the counsel to hear the question, but answer facing the Judges because they are the ones who make the decisions. I know it's a bit complicated, but if you would make that little extra effort, we would be grateful to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: As I explained, the lists indicated, not buildings, they indicated functions, so there are not 52 buildings on these lists. There are a number of functions that go beyond 52. I can't remember how many there are. So you would have under a location, you would have a mesjid is here, a mekteb is here and a gasulhane is here, but you don't know if you're talking about one building, two buildings or even eventually three buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, the list had geographic locations on it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you took those geographic locations as the universe of your study for the purposes of your testimony in this case; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were a couple of different lists, I should say, as I pointed out earlier, I was attentive to try to compare all information in order to see if something had been forgotten. Sometimes things are forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You compared different lists. Are these lists sometimes different, that is, they have different geographic sites on one list and not on another, or different cultural sites on one list that aren't on another?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: There are differences. In fact, there's a list for the Kiseljak municipality also supplied, also emanating from the Islamic community, which fails to mention that there is a mekteb in Bukve. It fails to mention that there's another mekteb in Donji Zezeljevo. There are differences. There are little differences, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question about these lists, Doctor. You said you received them and other materials prior to your testimony. Were they received by you, prior to your testimony, but after your on-site inspection in Central Bosnia, in May and June of 1994?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: They were before, before my on-site inspection. I have a lot to do, and I try to limit it. It takes a fair amount of time to find places in Central Bosnia, and so these materials were given to me before, and that helped me to organise my tours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before May of 1994?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no. I did a tour at the request of the Tribunal in April/May 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be specific here. You know that the Tribunal was established in November 1993. Try to be very specific in your responses to the Defence's questions.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think -- yes, I apologise. When I went to Central Bosnia in 1994, I had no lists given to me by anybody, except for the Riyaset. These were old lists that came out from the war. They were sort of everything in the kitchen sink is sort of put into them. The lists I'm talking about and you're asking questions about are specific lists given to me by the Tribunal last fall, I believe, and materials I saw last fall or January here. I used these in order to organise these trips that I have carried out in Central Bosnia from April to June 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trips were those?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It's about five, five day-trips all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photographs, which together constitute Exhibit 455, do they include photographs taken during your 1994 visit to the Lasva and Kiseljak valleys or during your 1998 visits, or are they a mixture of photographs from those various visits?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think I -- yes, there is a mixture. There are a few photographs from June 1994 and there are a few photographs taken in the April, June visits, and then there are other photographs, which are not my photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are some of the photographs also from your 1998 visits to the region?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are most of the photographs in Exhibit 455 from your 1998 visits, or are you able to make a generalisation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think there are probably more there, from the materials that the Tribunal supplied. We can go through every one of them and I can point out which ones are mine and which are the Tribunal's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So most of the Exhibit 455 were not taken by you and, therefore, you don't know when they were taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I would say about half of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Half of them were not taken by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, maybe a bit more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described the communities in the Kiseljak, Busovaca and Vitez municipalities as largely rural, small towns and the like. Did you find in your tours and inspections, that generally in these regions, residential districts are segregated by ethnic or religious groups?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It is a good question because the only answer to it is a nuanced one. Bosnian society was not the mix that the -- there's an idealic version of Bosnian society which has come out from the war, after the war, that it was a mix. In fact, if you look carefully at Bosnia or any particular region, if you look at towns, if you look at the countryside, you find it is not quite so simple. There are a lot of villages in the country which are mono-national or mono-ethnic. There are a few that are mixed. If you go to a town, and you take Stari Vitez. Stari Vitez is a Bosniak area inside of a town which is basically a Croatian town. In fact, there is a lot more segregation in the country than has often been said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that in the Lasva and Kiseljak valleys, generally villages are mono-ethnic, and where they are not mono-ethnic, within a village, residential districts are generally segregated by an ethnic or a religious group?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The villages that are on the hills are basically mono-ethnic. There is a little bit more mix in the valley, the main valley in Kiseljak. But I would basically agree with what you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This might be the moment, unless you have another question about the ethnic composition of the villages, this might be a good time to take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I've completed that area, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 2.30. The hearing is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.56 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, we're going to continue now with your cross-examination. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, good afternoon, Dr. Kaiser. You stated that mektebs generally resemble, from the outside, private residences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to recognise such a structure as a mekteb, you would have to have some local knowledge of the local sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: One has to ask questions to the local people. Sometimes the mihrab, that is, the prayer niche, is visible on the exterior wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, you have had some notes opened before you during your earlier testimony that you have referred to from time to time.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please feel free to continue to do so if it is helpful. If Exhibit 451 could be placed on the ELMO? That is one of the maps tendered by the Prosecution in connection with the testimony of this witness. Very well, you have it before you, Dr. Kaiser. You said, I believe, that the locations in yellow were under BiH army control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of what time?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I can answer you in terms of what I actually saw in 1994. I'd say that Kruscica, that was under ABiH control, because I was there; Stari Vitez, of course; Strane out in the east; and Merjani (phoen), I didn't go to, but it's visible from the road east in from the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't intend to make you go through them one at a time. My question, rather, was: Did you mark these in yellow because they were under BiH army control at the time of your visit in May and June of 1994 or did someone else mark these for you and tell you that they were under BiH army control at some point or points in time?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay. The way it works is this: Every single mosque, mekteb, or mesjid that was on the list and was indicated as severely damaged or destroyed I wanted to see. I saw these -- in fact, I didn't know exactly where all of these were located, and I simply made a list of them to go out and look for them, in fact. When I went to these areas, I could tell from the surrounding population that these were -- I presumed to be -- there was a Bosniak population in these areas, a big one. In some places I spoke with local people because I was uncertain as to where they could be. For example, Rovna, which is down here, I came along this road from the east here. I went up and I spoke -- there was nothing that was obvious there, not too many habitations in the area, not too many people, but up at the mosque there were some old men. I went and asked them some questions, and said, "Where was this during the war?" And they said to me, "This was in Armija territory." If you looked to see the damage, yes, that was possible. It's that kind of way, when you asked questions, I got the precise answer and I feel certain about those sites. The other ones I judged simply from the population. In some cases, you know, you are also going over front-line, and you know that you are going over the front-line, and that's the way you know where it is. It was not indicated to me that these were in Armija-controlled territory. I can tell you that. It was just by going around that I began to presume that they were, in fact, in Armija-controlled territory because of the population, because of what people said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made that judgement. Was that in May/June of '94 or in 1998 when you went back that you made the judgement that the locations in yellow were under BiH army control?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: You will remember that I only saw a few of these locations in 1994, so I made a judgement about certain of those locations. Kruscica was one of them. The other ones I mentioned at the beginning. In all the others, I made that judgement during the April to June trips around the areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: April to June 1998?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you learned that locations such as Jelinak, Putis and, perhaps, others had been in HVO territory during part of the war, what would that tell the court with respect to those locations?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I should say that I know that Jelinak and Strane were briefly in control. Jelinak I mentioned as an example of an inhabitant that said the village had been overrun in April 1994. I don't know how long it was overrun for. Putis, I didn't know that. I asked the local inhabitants, and I didn't get that answer. Strane looked as if it had been overrun because it had pillaged. Someone had gone in there. It was a Bosniak village, so I assumed it was the HVO. In a few cases I learned that it had happened, but I didn't include those as being in HVO-controlled territory simply because I didn't -- I knew that they weren't in HVO-controlled territory very long, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please make a break between the question and answer for the interpreters to catch up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, do you believe the court can or should infer anything from the fact, for example, that Jelinak and Strane were held by the HVO for a period of time, and yet there was little or no damage to cultural sites there; whereas, other sites that were under Croat control for longer periods of time and, thus, accessible to civilians, vandals, et cetera, they fared less well? Do you think that the court can or should make an inference based on that data?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it depends on how long something is under control. I don't know how long Jelinak was under HVO control, whether it was one day, two days or three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, ask your questions directly, please. Don't try to infer everything that the Judges might infer, because they are grown-up and know how to make the inferences that they need to make. Please don't make too many suggestions about any possible inferences that the Judges could make. Believe me, they will do what they have to do at the proper time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There must have been a problem in interpretation, Mr. President, because I wasn't suggesting the court's job or role. I apologise if it was interpreted in such a manner that the court understood me to be doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, can we reasonably infer that if the HVO held Jelinak for a few days or a week and a cultural site wasn't destroyed, then whatever HVO commander was on the ground there wasn't given any instructions or command, at least not one that he obeyed, to destroy a cultural site at that location?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The Jelinak case is an interesting case, if I can talk about that, because the head man of the village, he showed us his mekteb, mesjid, gasulhane, and he said that it had been overrun, fire had been set in it, and that it had been mined to go off. I have heard this thing about places being mined to go off, and at the last miraculous moment they didn't go off. Somebody took the mine out, et cetera. There were the slightest traces of fire. It was clear that the building had been rehabilitated. I put down it was lightly damaged. I don't know exactly how much damage was done to it, but to that building, there was an attempt made to damage it. But I don't know whether it was moderate or light, so I put light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the cultural site in Strane? Do you have any more for the court about that site?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think the village was overrun. There was a lot of pillaging. Explosives seems to have been put in houses. This little mesjid, this is a case of one that is visible from the outside, the mihrab, it was pillaged. It was pillaged. That was all. I don't know how long they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit 452 could be provided to the witness? That's the next in this series of maps. If it could be moved up so that the lower right-hand corner of the exhibit is visible on the ELMO, please, lower right-hand corner. Thank you. I think the exhibit is upside down, if it could be turned right-side up, please. Thank you very much. Dr. Kaiser, you said that the two locations in green had been hit by artillery from the east or south-east; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who held that territory during the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: One thing I should have mentioned to you, I also had mine maps, and that indicated often where forces were. Those mine maps I acquired from the Mine Action Centre in Sarajevo. In this case, if you take the mine map, you will find a whole line of mines north of the two towns here. I assume that this was, in fact, in Armija territory, these two locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who held the territory from which the direction of fire came causing the injury or damage to the sites?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: My inference, since it came from the north-east and south-east, generally from the easterly direction, my inference is that the damage would have been done by the Bosnian Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You discussed the causes of various damage visible to you. Am I correct that you were not in a position to differentiate between the effects of different types of explosives when exploded on or in a cultural site, or is that something that is within your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I would say that I can differentiate between artillery damage and explosives, high explosives. But, honestly, I could not tell you much, if anything, of technical nature about explosives used in a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whether military explosives, a mine, or civilian industrial explosives are used, you're not able to render an opinion on that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to allow myself to interrupt you for a moment. We are having a problem with the French transcript. We have to take a short break for a moment to correct the technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we are going to suspend the hearing for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Registrar, maybe you can tell us what is working and what isn't working.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We had a small transcript problem with the French, but everything is operating perfectly, or it seems to be operating perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I really admire your prudence. We can continue now, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, let me repeat my question which you were not given a chance to answer. Is it correct that you are not able to render an opinion in specific cases of -- the destruction of cultural sites whether military explosives, such as a mine, or whether other civilian explosive materials may have been used to cause a particular explosion or detonation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Regarding explosives put into buildings, I am not an expert and I cannot distinguish between a tank mine, a big charge of civilian explosives or other types of explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand with respect to the mosque in Kiseljak whether the minaret fell on the roof or did not fall on the roof. Do you need to see a photograph to refresh your recollection or can you answer the question without a photo?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I believe that some of the bricks fell on the roof, but you see a mass of bricks around the base of the minaret, outside. I don't think that the minaret was exploded in such a way as to fall on the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that that detonation was a "expert job." Do you mean it was expert in keeping the minaret from falling on the roof or was it done in an expert manner in some other way?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. I mean, it's an expert who made certain that it didn't fall on the roof. He put it somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: An expert could make it fall wherever he wanted it to fall. I think, I'm inferring that the artificer who put the explosives, in the minaret, in the Kiseljak mosque, he wanted the minaret to go in a certain direction and not another direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why would you do that?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't know. He could make more damage or less damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it in order to save the minaret, for instance?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: He wanted to destroy the minaret, there's no question about that, the question is about how much more damage he wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was an experiment on damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The opposite of what you do.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I couldn't do that, in other words, I would probably bring it down, maybe on top of the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the, I believe the phrase is, turbe, a tomb memorial of a sort. Where was that? Could you tell us the geographic location? I didn't catch that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The turbe which I mentioned is located in Gomionica Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was some information that it was the tomb of a commander of the Sultan's army.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain which sultan you're referring or the sultan of what empire?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Ottoman sultan, I mean, we're talking about Mohamed Fetih the second, I think, in the middle of the 15th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Donji Vecerska, you described a site that had the roof stripped, the roof tiles taken off. Can you tell the court, have you found in your studies of damage to cultural sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that there are different types of vandalism?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, there are different types of vandalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what those different types are?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, we have the trashing of the interior of a building, for example. That is upsetting everything. It's a spectrum, a spectrum of vandalism. It can be indiscriminate. It can be, for example, in the case of a church -- take an example of the churches from the Dubrovnik commune. There's a very famous example of vandalism which is carried out by the Serbian forces in Cilipi which involved cutting the heads off of statues of Mary and of Joseph and of another saint. That's a very specific kind of vandalism. There are other types of vandalism in churches, where the statue is knocked over, but nobody has gone to cut the head off. To go back to the spectrum of damage, there can be burning inside of a building, an attempt to burn it, to go to the exterior, we can shoot out or through stones through windows. We can take off a roof because, perhaps, one needs the tiles. Usually that's a good reason, otherwise it's a long job. This is sort of minor types of vandalism, not completely destructive of the structure. Then vandalism keeps going. I consider vandalism also to be burning and also putting explosive charges in a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also possible to categorise vandalism as, in the first category, the threat or removing of usable building materials apparently for the purpose of reuse as compared to vandalism that can be linked to the political or ethnic symbolic value of the thing being desecrated or vandalised. Is that a distinction that you, yourself, have made in the past, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I have made that distinction in the past. People have vandalised buildings in their own territory, of their own national group, or what they consider to be their own national group, because they are looking for tiles, because they are looking for wood to burn. Yes, I do make such a distinction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the unfinished mosque in Duhri and whether or not the minaret had, in fact, been constructed at all, despite reports that you received that there was a minaret at that location and that it had been destroyed. Would you agree that the general quality of hearsay reports in Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning destruction and vandalism and acts of violence, are quite poor, that is the quality of those hearsay reports are quite poor and, in fact, they are rather unreliable?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I believe that is to be the case. I pointed out also in these lists given by the Islamic community that the damage was systematically overestimated. This is true. You always have to go -- if you haven't got photographs, and then you have some good ones, you have to go and see something by yourself, because you cannot go upon the hearsay evidence. When I was working for the Council of Europe in 1993, and we were collecting all this material, on the basis on my own experience in 1992, the end of 1992 in Dubrovnik, these materials, I didn't know what to believe. It is a very, very difficult exercise. The same mistake can be repeated ten times. Yes, the hearsay evidence is not very good. I also mentioned that we thought that the good -- I read in a newspaper the Guca Gora monastery had been destroyed, and that's hearsay evidence and it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Guca Gora, were you not allowed inside because it was a BiH army installation, it was being used by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Precisely. I was not allowed inside because the Armija was in the establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was using it for their military purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Military purposes. I mean, it was presented to me -- in fact, it was also a form of protection. I did see what I thought to be mujahedeen in the area. I saw that the village, that Croats houses in that village had been burned. That seemed to me to be very, very convincing argument to put troops in the monastery to protect it from somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be assured that I'm not suggesting it was a good or a bad idea to have BiH army troops stationed in and around the monastery. Would you agree that you were not invited inside, not because they were guarding the monastery but because they were engaged in military activities inside the monastery?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think that what they knew and sensed is that I was nosing around to see what had happened, and the church had, in fact, been defiled in one way another. I mentioned that the graffiti was used. I think that's what they were afraid of me seeing. They were, perhaps, also afraid of me seeing that the soldiers were living in the monks quarters and had probably, my assistant didn't go into those quarters, but perhaps it was full of graffiti, insulting graffiti, because wherever soldiers go, there is often insulting graffiti and they didn't want me to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn, despite the limits put on your access, at the Guca Gora monastery, that some one-half of the vast library at that monastery had been destroyed by the mujahedeen when they took over the monastery in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That is news to me. I heard about the great fire at the end of World War II, supposedly carried out by the Germans. I was told by the Bosniak officials, in the municipality of Travnik, that much of the collection had been saved. Our cultural heritage assistant did not mention seeing traces of a fire, excuse me, the fire of a library. I'm not sure exactly what happened to the library and to the other treasures of Guca Gora. I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Doctor, would you please face us when you answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then tell the court, Doctor, if you recall, where you got the information in your report to the Council of Europe dated 16 March 1995 which reads: "Franciscan monastery at Guca Gora (Travnik): About 50 per cent of the library had been destroyed or lost during the period the monastery was occupied by mujahedeens in 1993, but ABiH managed to save part of it."

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Which report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 15 May 1995, Council of Europe, seventh informational report on war damage to the cultural heritage in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your update begins on page 37 and I was reading from the third paragraph under "Bosnia and Herzegovina" on page 39. Is that information you recall or you don't recall receiving it?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I recall -- well, I have in front of me the report from '94. I can't recall this particular information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the usher show the paragraph, first to the Prosecutor and then to the witness. This is the only copy I have. Perhaps it will refresh his memory, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand better. The question here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps we have made an error here. The sentence that you quoted, Mr. Hayman, the extract from the report of the Council of Europe is important. In the interpreter's mouth, I heard that they had been occupied by the HVO and then by the Bosnian army. The transcript mentions the Bosnian army. Could we repeat that sentence, please? I hope that doesn't bother you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will repeat it. It was not the HVO but the mujahedeens, who initially occupied the premises and then were replaced by the BiH army according to the report which managed then to save roughly one-half of the library holdings, the balance having been apparently destroyed by the mujahedeen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Dr. Kaiser, first of all, is your memory refreshed with respect to that bit of information?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I wrote it. I'm just trying to remember where I got it. I was in contact with ECMM, and this was information, I think, I probably got later on, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your the visit at which you were denied access to the monastery?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, after the visit, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is -- I did accurately read a portion of your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If Exhibits 66/2 and 66/3 could be provided to the witness, they pertain, I believe, to the Svinjarevo mesjid.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Mesjid, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was a little confused, Doctor, I thought you said, but correct me if I'm wrong, that these photos depicted damage to this mosque, but that in a later photo you saw potential damage from burning, or evidence of burning, but not in these photos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I have photos that I took in which the burning -- the smoke is quite clear, is quite clearly on certain objects. It's clear at the base of the mihrab here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is clear?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Right here. I'm not sure that I can say that that's smoke damage there actually. Then there is another storey, there is another floor, and there is a staircase. Underneath the staircase, there are the traces of fire, of smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you saw in 1998?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: 1998. Also, there are other pictures that I have, in which certain elements of the roof, in fact, are damaged by fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also photos from 1998?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that damage is not apparent in these photos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No, it's not apparent in those photos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if these photos -- excuse me. Let's pause for a moment. If these photos were taken in 1996 and you found burning damage in 1998, that would tell us, of course, that that subsequent damage occurred during that interval; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm completed with those photos, Mr. Usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the court of several items of information you received concerning when specific cultural sites were damaged. Am I correct that you have no other information concerning the time or circumstances of the damage to the various sites you have reviewed, other than what you have already told the court?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Basically, that's correct. There may be a few other notations in reports that I have made, but basically, this is all the information. There's not very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any basis to give the court an opinion whether the majority of the damage to the sites you have discussed occurred after the Washington Agreement in roughly March 1994 or occurred before the Washington Agreement in 1994, March of that year?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, clearly if the only information I have is here, I cannot put specific dates on the damage which has been done to these buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning your attention to Exhibit 451, which is the map with a large number of yellow locations indicated, if that could go back on the ELMO, please. Is it your believe, Doctor, that these locations in yellow were certainly, that is, cultural sites indicated by the locations in yellow on Exhibit 451, were certainly within the range of HVO artillery during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Can I be a little boring here and go one by one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only the court can grant you leave in that area, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay. For example, well, obviously, the Stari Vitez, the mosque there was quite visible. Bukve is very visible from the main road. Sadovaci, this is different. This, by the way, was undamaged. I don't think this building was visible to HVO positions. Preocica, I think the mosque is visible. Dolovici, it's visible to the front-line positions of the HVO. Sivrino Selo, yes. Vrhovine, I doubt very much if the mesjid is visible. There is, by the way, another mosque here in Poculica, which I don't know why I didn't put it on which is visible as undamaged. The mosque in Vrhovine, I'm not sure if that is visible. Kruscica, the mosque, I think, was visible. The mesjid was not visible and is not damaged. Vreniske, I really don't think it's visible. It was in a valley. Rovna, visible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was this last one damaged or not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Vreniske, not damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was not visible to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No. Rovna was visible, it had slight damage. Besici, this is visible and was damaged. Jelinak was definitely visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it damaged?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it was damaged, yes. Putis, I think, was visible from the hill here. I believe there was fighting in this hill. Strane, it's in the trees. It's a very small building. I'm not sure if it was visible. Merdjani may have been visible at one moment or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we conclude that the sites you identified as visible, to HVO artillery, nonetheless, showed no other indications of having been targeted and damaged by HVO artillery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, I think Bukve was targeted. Stari Vitez was targeted. Kruscica was targeted once. It had one impact in it. Wait a minute, Preocica, was targeted once, one mortar shell, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if the witness can finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I thought he had finished.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, Rovna was targeted, not by artillery or mortars, though. It was hit by small arms. Besici was hit by small arms and maybe by projectiles, but not big projectiles. Jelinak was not hit by projectiles. Putis was shot by -- small arms damage, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Doctor, if any of these visible sites, if targeted by an artillery attack directed at the site, by capable artillery operators, the site could be totally destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: There's no doubt about it. I mean, a capable artillery man, if he decides to go after something, he can get it, he can hit it badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw that result in hundreds of cases with respect to the Bosnian Serb army; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, maybe I didn't see the case for hundreds of front-line -- mosques near the front-line, but I saw many cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you see here is different; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you compared damage to Muslim and Catholic sites. Let me ask you just a few examples. Was the Catholic church in Vitez damaged by fire? When I say "fire," I mean projectile fire?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it was, in fact. Not seriously, but it was damaged, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the damage comparable to the pock marks on the Stari Vitez mosque?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it's a little less. I think it's one or two impacts on the church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mortar impacts?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay, I don't have pictures in front of me, I don't remember, but not heavy artillery. It wasn't a big artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have made general comparisons between Muslim and Catholic sites, let me ask you, on the list that the Prosecutor's office passed on to you for your 1998 review, were there any Catholic sites or were those exclusively Muslim or Islamic religious sites?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No, they were exclusively Islamic sacral and educational buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any damage to Catholic sites in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I have not been in that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Vlajkovica?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: This village is close to a group of schools that UNESCO is working on, and I have gone through that area. But about a year ago, I wasn't involved in sacral buildings at the time. I think the village was damaged. I can't remember exactly what the state of the church was, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Restovsko in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't think there's very much -- I don't recall seeing any damage to the church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The church in Silos near Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I'm wondering, is that the same church we were talking about? There is one church in Kacuni. I mean, there's only one church I can recall on the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. The description I have is of the villages on the road from Fojnica to Kiseljak, east of Fojnica is Natbare, afterwards is mainly Croat Silo, largely burnt out, along with it recent Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's from my report from June 1994. That's the road from Fojnica to Kiseljak. It's not Kacuni to Kiseljak. Yes, I remember going through that area and seeing a Catholic church that was damaged, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was burned out?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Burned out, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the psychological impact on a population, civilian population, as well as individual soldiers, would you agree that the psychological impact of destruction to religious sites is a common one among various religious or ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Can you rephrase that? I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the impact on a population, be it a Muslim population, a Catholic population, or some other religious group, it is the same when one's own group's religious sites are destroyed, targeted, and are the victims of violence?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for rephrasing your question. Yes, it is the same, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also believe that that psychological impact crosses municipal lines, that, for example, acts of violence in a neighbouring municipality may heighten fear, paranoia, anxiety in the next door municipality?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you visit Bugojno on any of your tours or visits to the Central Bosnia region?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: My tour in 1994, I went through it, but unfortunately, since then I've been back, and not just to go through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, Bugojno is a very nasty place, to put it bluntly, even speaking as a UNESCO representative. There was a case of a big church out there, an explosive being set at the foot of it. This is after Dayton. The church in Humac and this was the most extraordinary kind of violence to have seen since the war, was the victim of an explosive charge, which destroyed the church tower. This was about a year ago, before the elections. Bugojna is not a very nice place. It is a very, very badly vandalised Catholic cemetery which I have written about to the Reis Ul Uleima, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the former Croat population of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: They have had a very, very tough time there. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to visit Fojnica and, if so, what did you find?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I visited Fojnica only once. I visited during the June 1994 mission. It seemed to be in rather bad condition. I didn't -- this was a town in which the monitors didn't want me to get out of the vehicle, even though it was in Armija territory. They pointed out to me that there had been a certain amount of ethnic cleansing of the Croatian population. We were visiting the monastery in Fojnica, because the monastery in Fojnica has a very, very important, very rich collection, and, of course, I knew about the incident in the monastery, I guess which was in October '93, in which two priests had been assassinated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't know who they were assassinated by, but I don't assume they were assassinated by other Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the former Croat population of Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: When, during the war or after the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find the situation when you visited?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It looked like a very unhappy place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few more questions, Doctor, but not many. In the area of responsibility, you said that the JNA taught the dictates of The Hague convention, well. Do you know what they taught? Have you seen teaching materials? Were you in the JNA, Doctor, or are your sources of information something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think there is four questions there as opposed to one. I have to ask council to break his questions down, it might be easier for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us your source of information for your knowledge of what the former JNA, at a particular point in time, did or did not teach concerning The Hague conventions?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, this is, of course, a general statement. This is an evaluation from within UNESCO. UNESCO is involved in the implementation of The Hague convention. It is responsible for keeping the archives. They are supposed to know something about the implementation with the armed forces. You would call this hearsay evidence but it's from inside UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ultimate source, other than the general believe on UNESCO's part?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't work in that area. I haven't seen the materials of the reports that were compiled. The thing is that, Yugoslavia compiled reports and sent them, regularly, to UNESCO. They do exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break-up of the former Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any reports after the break-up and after the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't know. I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would doubt it because the situation became somewhat chaotic; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does The Hague treaty require the flying of a particular flag, over sites that are registered as being of cultural significance?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I believe that it recommends it. If you don't fly it, then you're taking a risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, if you fly it and the building is destroyed, then you haven't violated the treaty; is that right? You haven't violated your duty to protect the building; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: You have respected the recommendation. You have respected the spirit of the convention. You have allowed the enemy to make his choice. Remember, it depends on the enemy and whether he wants to shoot or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think, in Central Bosnia, during the war that was fought there, it was a good idea for any party to put up flags identifying particular sites or do you think that the failure to fly such flags was a reasonable exercise of discretion by whatever local civil authorities made that decision?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I doubt very much that there any flags in Central Bosnia. The flags were usually put up, for example, in Croatia. They were put up by the institutes to preserve cultural heritage. Croatia had an excellent network of those. Bosnia had a poor network. Would it have been a good idea to put them up in the war? It seems one of the lessons that this war has taught us is that these flags didn't protect very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, you think it's unlikely they had any flags to begin with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it's unlikely, probably, in this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of the duty of military personnel with respect to listed sites. Is it your opinion that military personnel had a duty to act as civil police and physically guard registered sites during wartime? Is that your understanding of The Hague convention?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: One of the understandings is they don't give orders to shoot at buildings. That's one thing. Secondly, if they regard that there is a danger to a building from military personnel or armed personnel, I believe that they cannot -- they don't necessarily have to put soldiers in front of it. Well, they can put military police in front of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They have an obligation to attempt to maintain discipline within their own troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the obligation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, that's one of the obligations, yes. If necessary, to protect the building. I've asked SFOR to protect buildings, in fact, in the post-Dayton situation, if necessary, with troops, by patrols. I think it's also a solution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've spoken, though, of a legal duty. Can you articulate what that legal duty is for military personnel under The Hague conventions or is that outside your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, you will imagine, sir, that I would like The Hague convention to be respected. Unfortunately, I have seen it hasn't been so respected, and not very much respected during the war. I don't want to say I'm cynical about The Hague convention, but I certainly approve of everything that's being done to reform it. In a certain sense, I'm not so interested in what it has to say, but I am interested in the spirit of it. The question is what should the soldiers do? The commanders should give orders to their soldiers to respect certain buildings. They should list the buildings. We're talking about, in combat situations. Outside combat situations, they should make -- they should try to ensure that those orders are, in fact, respected and that soldiers don't do something, if they feel that there is a situation they can't control so well, then they should, if necessary, guard the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking now about buildings within the area of control of a particular military force, as opposed to buildings outside of that area?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a military commander gives orders, repeated orders, to his forces to respect and protect civilian structures, is that consistent with the duties, as you understand them, arising on the part of military commanders under The Hague convention?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It's a good start. At least the soldiers know what they are up against if they disrespect the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a soldier at a lower level disrespects that order, is the commander responsible for a criminal offence under The Hague conventions? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: If a soldier disrespects the order, and his commander does nothing to be certain to see that he is punished, then his commander has a responsibility, but the commander is not necessarily responsible for what the subordinate soldier does. He is responsible to make certain that he is punished for it, if he has done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, let me remind you that the witness has come to testify about a certain number of things. I'm not sure that his opinions on military command responsibility are moving a little bit away from the purpose of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have two more questions on this area, Mr. President. He did give an opinion on the responsibility of commanders and if I may, I would like to finish the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it then, Doctor, your understanding is the obligation on the part of military commanders created under The Hague convention, is not one of strict liability?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Is not one of strict liability?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It is not a strict liability obligation on the part of a military commander?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I may be a bit thick. Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. This is precisely the point, I believe, that Your Honour has just addressed on the issue of strict liability and what it means within the term of international law and international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: He gave a legal opinion, Mr. President, he gave a legal opinion on the duties of civil authorities and military authorities. I don't know what I'm supposed to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have to say that you are taking the words out of my mouth, but I'm also going to turn to the Prosecution. When you ask too much of a witness, you then expose yourself to have questions that go beyond the limits. I have said, the witness comes to express what he knows about a specific area. Dr. Kaiser, perhaps not theoretically, perhaps not an expert in military responsibility. All right, let's leave it at that. You have asked your questions, Mr. Hayman. Have you got any others that you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One more and then one last area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before asking to opine, were you shown any orders of my client?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said during your May/June 1994 visit, you could not get out of your car in Kiseljak or take pictures because it was too dangerous. Why was it too dangerous. This was after the cease-fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, this was the opinion of the ECMM. I was under their control. I would not question it. I think they believed that what we could call -- there was an expression that was used a lot during the war, it's uncontrollable elements, and ECMM's opinion was that there were significant uncontrollable elements in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you that uncontrollable elements in Kiseljak were omnipresent?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you who these uncontrollable elements were and whether they had been there during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember -- the uncontrollable elements were Croat elements. They didn't enter into a long history about what they had done or not done during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
