utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree with the following, referring to acts of vandalism and violence perpetrated on cultural sites in Bosnia-Herzegovina: "These acts of vandalism are perpetrated --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, what page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Report of 19 January, 1994, page 17, paragraph 64.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "These acts of vandalism are perpetrated by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you read more slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "These acts of vandalism are perpetrated by representatives of authority, soldiers and military and probably civilian police. It can be posited that they are sometimes deliberately ordered by local authorities but that many of them are spontaneous." Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask, then, if you agree with the following, paragraph 65: "The sense of this term," referring, I believe, to spontaneous, "Should be elucidated. HVO and BiH units are armies of civilians, sometimes led by ex-JNA officers, but often led by other civilians. The lack of discipline, combined with the suffering that many of these soldiers have known, either to themselves, directly in prison camps or occupied areas or to their families and their property, has caused an extremely dangerous force for prisoners, civilians, and property. Moreover, they are encouraged to commit outrages by political and military leaders who envisage Bosnia-Herzegovina as a series of small, pure ethnic states." Do you agree with that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us, to tell this court, whether it's your belief that all political and military leaders on the BiH army and HVO side encouraged persons or soldiers to commit outrages, or was it a subpopulation of that group, namely, only some leaders of any stripe that engaged in such activity?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it was only some leaders. I don't think it was all leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, do you want to redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you very much. Re-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just asked a series of questions by counsel concerning the destruction of cultural and sacral monuments being sanctioned by HVO politicians and leaders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked that series of questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that it was done by some leaders and not by others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, by that, that there within the HVO structure, there were moderate leaders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please slow down. Think about the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, are you saying that within the Croat population, there were moderate leaders?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as moderate military leaders?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you likewise saying that within the HVO military, there were more extreme leaders, both political and military, within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think that was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted that there were almost 69 per cent of the sacral buildings within Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak which were destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, from moderate damage to complete destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moderate damage to complete destruction?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of which were completely dynamited. Now, that's well over half, and then the balance were damaged in a slight way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these areas, there was a significant amount of ethnic cleansing of the Bosnian Muslim population, was there not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you think was winning the day, the military commanders who were attempting to eradicate the Muslim population or the military commanders that wanted some type of coexistence?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The former not the latter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's pretty clear when you look at the evidence in that area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked some questions, both on direct, but some additional questions by counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please speak slowly, otherwise, once again I'm going to ask that we take a break for the interpreters because we can't go on that way. It's going too fast. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do apologise, Mr. President. I will attempt to slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by counsel concerning the obligations of military commanders, as well as the record keeping that was done by the JNA, prior to the fall of the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On JNA maps, do they not have religious facilities marked on those maps or do you know?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I've not had, in my hands, a JNA map, but on the maps that we are using for going around, the religious facilities are clearly marked. I find it very hard to imagine that it is not clearly marked on the JNA map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you conclude that JNA-trained officers knew that religious sacral and cultural monuments were not to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think they knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about a few issues raised by Mr. Hayman, and let us start, if you will, with the Guca Gora situation. You commented in your -- pardon me for a moment, 31 August 1994 report concerning the issues in Guca Gora and the reported damage in Guca Gora. I read to you, did you not say this that: "The least bad solution under the present circumstances is that the ABiH remain in the ensemble until the return of the Franciscans can be assured, along with the stationing of an adequate police guard."

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Those are my words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not also say, when talking about the Fojnica monastery, again, counsel, this is on page 14 of the 31 August 1994 report, and you recount the killing of the two Franciscan priests in November of 1993, did you not also say that the monastery presently has a BH guard, police guard?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the feeling, during your research and years in the former Yugoslavia, that the Bosnian Muslim authorities had sensitivity to the destruction -- or Bosnian Muslim people as a whole, had a sensitivity to the destruction of sacral monuments and sacral buildings?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I have come to believe that, both from the war experience and also afterward. I remember, this is after the war, there's a little village near Novi Travnik called Pecine which is up in the hills. It's very far away from everywhere. It's a Croat village. I had information that in December, December 1996, I think, that this church had been torched, and I went up there, you know, you had to go up with a 4-wheel drive vehicle, winding, winding, winding road, nobody there, nobody there. I went into the village, and I did, indeed, find that the church had been torched. To my astonishment, I also found two Bosniak policeman who had been stationed up there to make certain that it wasn't completely torched. This is a post-war example. If you go back to the war, you will see in the various towns on the -- the front-line towns, that the authorities had done much, it seems, to make certain that the Orthodox churches and the Catholic churches were not abused. They didn't always succeed. Some places are very bad, and I'm not too surprised in towns that are shelled every day, you know, 20 or 30 rounds, that somebody goes and torches the Orthodox church. There was a case, I think, in Maglaj. It was quite striking that there seemed to be an effort on the part of the authorities, on many of the Bosniak authorities, to take care of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the actual soldiers on the ground? Did you have any instances you might relate to the Chamber concerning the feeling of the rank and file among the Armija concerning the destruction of Catholic institutions? I point you to what you relayed to me concerning Dolac.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: In a certain sense, you know, very uncontrollable situation, leaders can say something in the capital, and then a local leader may have a totally different opinion, and the local leader cannot have complete control and something happens somewhere else. What I'm saying is a lot of things will rest on the individual soldier. It's true in Dolac, when I went to look at the church in Dolac, it was in June 1994, it was somewhat vandalised, not dramatically damaged, and I remember always a soldier, a Bosniak soldier from the Krajine, and he was a refugee, carrying a load of wood. He walked past us and he began sort of shouting at me. He said, "Why aren't you going down to the Lasva valley and looking at the dynamited mosques? Why are you looking always at the churches here?" And then he pointed at the church, and he said, "This is the house of God. We will not destroy it." This was what was interpreted to me. And I was rather struck by that remark. I have always been struck by it and I've had to think about it since and what did it mean? Did it mean that the rural Bosniak was more respectful of cultural heritage than the rural Croat or the rural Serb? What did it mean? Because when he pointed out the church to me in that condition, I mean, that's what it looked like, that there was a respect for the religious object of the other faith. It's a very difficult thing to objectively analyse, weigh and compare the Croatian soldier, the Serbian soldier and the Bosniak soldier, et cetera, et cetera,. But I think when the inventories are finally completed on what happened to sacral heritage, one will find out that there was one side that did behave better than the other sides. Why was that? I'm always turning that one around and maybe I'm starting to find some answers to it. Excuse me, I'm not being very clear. In this war, people are always looking for simple answers. There were people outside in the international community who said that, they are all a bunch of savages so we don't go and intervene. Then there were other ones who said, oh, no, no, it was a fantastic place, they loved each other throughout their history they lived together, et cetera, et cetera, and the truth is somewhere between. If you look at Islam, Islam has a special relationship to the Christian religion, a relationship that the Christians do not have with the Islam religion. Islam is a younger religion than Christianity, and Christians, Jews, are so-called people of the book. Our prophets are also the prophets under Islam. So there is a special kind of relationship, special attitude of Islam towards Christians. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there's something else, is that the Turks, the Ottoman Empire controlled the area for four centuries. It was an empire of relative degree of tolerance, not sort of -- there's been a lot of said about how tolerant it was. It was fairly tolerant compared to many Christian monarchies of the period. In other words, I think that there's a kind of activism on the part of the Bosniaks. They tolerate, they have a history of tolerating the other religions. They were powerful. It's a memory of a power, of their society, of the civilisation, the Ottoman civilisation there in Bosnia. It's a long, long memory of it. It's a sense, although it doesn't manifest itself that way, a kind of a sense of superiority, this respect and tolerance. And I think to a degree, that Christians whether they be Catholic or Orthodox, too have not forgotten something. They have not forgotten that they were tolerated. They have a different relationship. As I say, I'm sort of thinking out loud, I'm looking for reasons why it happened this way, because I don't believe necessarily that Sarajevo could give an order and it would be respected everywhere. Something deeper in individual people, and whatever the reasons, it is something of value, and wherever it occurred, whatever Serb or Croat or Bosniak, it's of value. With respect to cultural heritage, when the final inventory is drawn up, I think it will be shown that the Bosniaks behaved better than the other sides. I wrote that in 1994, and today I still believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of follow-up questions, Doctor, concerning some questions asked to you on cross-examination. The first has to do with the lists that were provided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would ask you to answer the questions, not to go beyond the scope of the questions, because in respect of the Defence, it could be thrown off balance. Generally, you must answer the questions directly. Try to answer as specifically as you can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you were asked some questions about this list of Islamic sites that was given to you by a representative from the Office of the Prosecutor, from the Islamic institute in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that list correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I pointed out that there were a few little problems with the list, but I believe it is basically 95 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct your own survey of those sites, in that you viewed the sites and made your own determinations concerning completely destroyed, seriously damaged, lightly damaged, or was that a decision that was made to you by some other institution?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No, I checked what was on the list presented by the Islamic community. Nobody else told me to go there or not to go there or whatever, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made your own decisions?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you to take a look at Exhibit 390A. This is a map that has been received in evidence which is a view of Gomionica, if you could put that on the ELMO, please? You testified previously that there was a mekteb in Gomionica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that designated as point 3?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a couple of questions by Defence counsel concerning the identification of mektebs, and I believe you said, both in cross and in direct, that often from the outside a mekteb is difficult to identify; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you then said in cross-examination that sometimes you can see the outline of the mihrab on the mekteb?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly could you not identify a Islamic sacral site if you went inside?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other side, if you take a look at Exhibit 390, you were asked some questions about a turbe in Gomionica. Is that designated in point 2?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Exhibit 390? Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm done with that exhibit. If we can turn our attention to the maps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, do you have many questions? This is in order for us to organise our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just start on this first map, 451? Doctor, you identified these areas on Exhibit 451, as basically, front-line positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, in front-line zones, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Front-line zones.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally, soldiers in front-line zones are pretty busy, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, it depends if -- yes, they can be very busy. Sometimes they are just waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your questions directly, Mr. Kehoe. We could assume that soldiers are occupied with things. Ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there is fighting going on in these areas, and trenches are being laid in these areas, one would assume that the soldiers in the trenches are busy; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Defending themselves or engaging in an offensive?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Of course, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two maps that you gave us, Exhibits 353 and 354, the maps where the various locales are designated as being destroyed in HVO territory in varying capacities, they are within HVO lines, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the most significant damage that you observed was done in areas that was within the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to consult with my colleagues for a moment. The interpreters are going to be the judges now. They are the ones who take the decision. I've consulted with my colleagues. We have about 20 or 25 minutes of questions that the Judges want to ask, depending, of course, on how the answers are given. Then I think that there are no other witnesses, is that correct, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, that's correct, Mr. President. This is the last witness for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the interpreters are tired. In light of their fatigue, would they like to take a break immediately and then come back for the 25 minutes or would they prefer that we finish now? For once, we're going to bow to the interpreters' will. I think we're going to take a break. There has to be unanimity here. There is no unanimous consensus, then we take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in. We will now resume the hearing for the questions the Judges would like to ask. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me first turn to Judge Riad. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Kaiser. I would like to have some more information from you. That was very informative testimony, but I would like to have the benefit of your knowledge. Perhaps if you are in a position to answer me, because sometimes it might be beyond your scope, although you are really here in two capacities. You are an expert on cultural heritage, and you have the ground experience of what happened. So in light of these two main backgrounds, I'll ask you my questions. You first went to Bosnia in June 1994 and then April 1998. You went twice?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Your Honour, I went in May/June 1994 on a mission with the ECMM for the Council of Europe. I have since been back. I worked a lot in Mostar from the fall of 1994 to the summer of 1995. In October 1995, I became a representative of UNESCO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm there all the time since October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All the time?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then you are really an eyewitness. I'm speaking of the list that was given to you from ICTY in April 1998. You verified the damage done to certain sites. Now, this damage was done in 1994 or 1993. It was done before. Would this lapse of time increase the damage or would it make it worse or would it make it better if it were repaired?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Of course it makes it worse. When the roof is damaged, the rain is coming in and the ceiling is rotting. If the building has been damaged by explosives and it has not been attended to, the damage gets worse, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In your opinion, much of it was repaired or much of it had deteriorated more?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, let's say that the mosque, mesjids and mektebs, which are in the territory controlled by Armija, many of them have been repaired if they were damaged. In the other territory, if they had been damaged, they have not been repaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the places occupied by the HVO, nothing has been repaired?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Nothing has been repaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nothing has been repaired.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: With one exception, one exception. In Rotilj, the mekteb, in fact, wasn't damaged. It wasn't damaged by HVO soldiers. It was damaged by refugees, in fact, who lived in it, so there's a totally different kind of damage, and that has been repaired, but that was the only case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of the damage, you mentioned there were several degrees of damage. Would you consider that -- you said that, among other things, there was no minaret standing in HVO territory. Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you consider that there was something systematic in trying to make all these minarets disappear?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Systematic?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: If they all went, there was something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not individual endeavours, by angry, angry, indigenous people of the police.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Angry, indigenous people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Of the villages, just each one trying to destroy something.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: To destroy a minaret, you need explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, and they were destroyed in some kind of a homogenous manner. You mentioned some of it was lying in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I believe that usually the explosives were set by people who are professionals, they knew what they were doing. In a few cases, not, but usually yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By experts. And by heavy weapons, heavy mines, heavy explosives?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Well, enough explosive to do the job. It's sort of a graduated scale, I think. It was well-dosed to do what was necessary. It depends on whether the building materials are brick, whether they're concrete, whether they're stone. It depends on the building materials you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was by professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Most of the time, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would you rule out the fact that all of these minarets would have been destroyed in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: When you're fighting, you're doing something else. You are not shooting -- there is no point to shoot at a mosque, unless it's being used militarily. There's no reason to do so. I don't think that in fighting that the mosques were damaged. As I pointed out, there was very, very little damage from military means on the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they were aimed at specifically? It was a specific damage, not casual damage done in fighting?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: The mining of the minarets was specific destruction, yes, outside of the fighting. It was by firing -- if you burnt the mosque that had a minaret in the roof like Han Ploca, that minaret fell through. If you have a brick or a cement, reinforcing-steel structured minaret, you use mines or some other explosives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of damage, you said that the sacral Muslim heritage was severely or totally damaged in Vitez, severely or totally damaged in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Okay, Vitez municipality under HVO control, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was, let's say, the stronghold of the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There was no protection from the authorities, because you mentioned an example of Pecine village where you went and the monastery was protected by two soldiers, by two BiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Two BiH policemen after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: After the war?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But to prevent damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there anything like that in Vitez, the protection of the sites of the sacral Muslim heritage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: During the war, you're asking?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whenever you went.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I did not see any protection of the sites. They were all damaged. There were no policemen. There were no soldiers around them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they were all damaged?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, the ones I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said "totally or severely damaged," to quote you right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you have to fly a flag in order to indicate that it is a religious site or a cultural site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it is recommended that you have to do so. Normally, the lists are supposed to be communicated between two warring sides. So even if you don't fly the flag, they are supposed to know where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you think that you should also fly a flag on a minaret or does it speak for itself?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: To fly a flag to protect it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To protect a minaret, is it compulsory? If there's no flag on the minaret --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Whether or not there's a flag on the minaret doesn't matter. You are not supposed to shoot at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are not supposed to shoot at it. I think I have one more question for you. You went through many details. I think I'm well-informed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Of course, if you have any additional questions, you can ask them whenever you like, once your colleague or myself have asked our questions. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, would I be write in compartmentalising your testimony this way: There is a general part in which you spoke to us very engagingly, if I may say so, of the need which all communities feel to identify themselves by one method or another, and there is a specific part in which you told us of your observations in Bosnia, and you sought to relate that to the general part. Would that be a correct appreciation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's a very generous appreciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us take the general part. Would I be right in understanding you this way: That all communities have a common need to identify themselves. They may do so by one method or another, and some communities may place greater reliance on one method than another?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, these methods would include, history, culture, religion, religious buildings, and religious objects, among others; am I right?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us take history. You did your doctoral thesis in France?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I did it in London but it was French history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm glad for the correction, but it doesn't blank the point I am about to put to you and it is this: With no disrespect to one country or another, would I be right in saying that the body of historical writing in, say, France about France is of greater density and larger proportion than the corresponding body of history in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Where the levels of historical writing differ, would I be correct to say that a community which disposes of a lower level of historical writing would tend to place greater reliance on religious buildings, religious objects, cultural artefacts for the purpose of meeting this common need, which all communities feel, to identify themselves?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think that would be a reasonable hypothesis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right in saying that in Bosnia, the infliction of damage on a religious building would tend to perpetrate a greater sense of injury on the perception by people of its own identity than in the case of a country which could place greater reliance on its sense of history?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That could be the case. But, for example, after World War I in France, which already in 1918 had a very, very, very long and extensive rich written memory, the necessity to rebuild churches destroyed in bombardments was felt very strongly, and enormous resources were put into rebuilding hundreds of churches. So what you're saying could be so, but it would have to be nuanced as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yes, indeed, that would be so, but I'm concerned not with the absolute need felt by people to repair buildings, but the relativity’s involved. Let us go to the question of mono-ethnic villages. I understood you to be saying that, yes, there were many villages in Bosnia which were mono-ethnic. Would I be right in understanding you to mean this: That a village which was mono-ethnic in the sense of being composed of Croats could, nevertheless, co-exist in the same region with another village which was mono-ethnic in the sense of being composed of, say, Serbs or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you draw a distinction between a situation where, within one region, you have a case of coexistence of different mono-ethnic villages on one side, and on the other side a region which consists entirely of mono-ethnic villages?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I would draw a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You would. If the evolution moved from the former to the latter situation, then I understand your testimony to mean that a change would be perpetrated on the identity of both peoples; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us move to the question of reprisals. It's a word you used. I, myself, will not repeat it to you in any more technical sense than that in which you may have employed it. Would I be correct in understanding you to mean this: Yes, on the side of the Bosniaks, there were instances in which damage was done to Catholic places of religious worship and so on, but that that was done by way of reprisals in the sense of ad hoc, retaliatory action; is that a way of understanding your evidence, or should I understand that to mean that this signified the adoption by the Bosniaks also of a policy of ethnic separation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think there's a problem of calendars and chronologies that always has to be sorted out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: -- in these cases, otherwise, you don't know whether something is a reprisal or not. That's the answer to the first part of your question. The second part of your question: Is there an evolution towards a solution on all parties of mono-ethnicity in the war? I believe that is what you're saying. I'm looking now across a perspective of the piece, and I would say across a perspective of the piece, I think that is happening. It was probably happening in the war, too, in certain areas, also in Armija-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So that was the de facto position. Was that also the policy of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I don't think it was. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you told us, if I may translate your terms, of a religious predisposition on the part of the Bosniaks to regard with a certain degree of respect Catholic places of worship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You told us of seeing ABiH soldiers or policemen guarding Catholic places of worship which had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: In a few cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you ever see on the other side any HVO soldiers or policemen guarding damaged Bosniak buildings of worship?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: After the war, yes, but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Not during the war?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Not during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us stick to the period of the war. Was this a matter of public knowledge that ABiH soldiers and policemen were guarding and protecting Catholic places of worship which had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I can't really answer that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us talk a little about Bugojno. You saw, I think, some damage to a Catholic place of worship, did you?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you had occasion to write to the Uleima?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: For the purposes of the record, am I right in saying that the Uleima is a learned, religious gentleman --

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: -- in a leadership position?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, he is the leader of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What was his reaction; do you know?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: He did not write back to me, but I heard he was furious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Furious about your writing to him or furious about the damage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: He thought I should be taking much more interest in Muslim cemeteries and not raising this problem of the Catholic cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Then I thank you. That is the last question I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That was your last question. I'm going to ask you only a few questions, and then my colleague, Judge Riad, may have one or two questions to ask, and then you will be finished. I might ask you somewhat of an indiscreet question. Were any other studies done on the question of cultural destruction? Do you direct thesis? Do you know students who might be working in that area or, perhaps, any other researchers elsewhere in the world that would be interested in that aspect of the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: During the war, Dr. Marion Wenzel, who is a noted specialist of the country, especially of the Stezi (phoen), you will find her reports also with the Council of Europe. She was also involved with this. I'm afraid I'm not aware of many initiatives during the war outside of the Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was a tendency to put into circulation lists of damaged heritage which were totally uncontrollable and not very, very useful. After the war, yes, there's a big interest after the war in the damage of cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. If I've understood you correctly, the mektebs are not very easily distinguishable from the churches or the mosques. In your opinion, in order to destroy them in any systematic fashion, in a well-targeted fashion, in your opinion, would you say that you would have to be a soldier who comes from that area in order to spot them quickly?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, it's true in the case of the mektebs and in the case of some mesjids. You wouldn't necessarily know what it is, and you would have to come from the area in order to do so. For the mosques, that's an obvious thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you think that the destruction might have been caused by civilians, civilians that were not under the control of the military personnel, for example, who had been inflamed by propaganda? Do you think that would be possible?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Absolutely. The one photograph that I showed of the roof being stripped, the bottom part of the roof, I think that was probably done by civilians who needed those tiles. There are other types of damage, for example, in a mekteb in Dolci. There is a very poor burning attempt on the floor which doesn't show very much determination. I think maybe that could even be children who attempted to fire it. Adults might be more determined. Soldiers would be better equipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. From the point of view of proportions, without being particularly specific but in a general fashion, in the type of vandalism that you noticed, were there more ritualistic types of vandalism than others? My second question, I have two, if "yes," were your observations something that would lead you to think that what was involved with was a ritualistic vandalism? I know my question was long. Let me say it again: First of all, are there ritualistic types of vandalism? For example, in a Catholic church, one might shell the walls of the church. That's a ritualistic vandalism. But if you were to go into the tabernacle and pull out the hostises and throw them on the ground, that would be a ritualistic act of vandalism which would be even stronger. In the destruction that you noted, were you able to see that, in general, people went to the very heart of the ritual and to the very heart of the religious symbolism?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Dealing with the destruction of a Catholic church by Serbs, there is so much similarity in religions that you know where to go and what to destroy. When it comes to dealing with an Islamic building, I'm not so certain that the Christians know as well. I've seen a few cases where, perhaps, a ritual is made up by those who did the destruction, that is, a setting of fire in the mihrab, which we would all know points towards Mecca. In the case, possibly, of the Kiseljak mosque, if you look at the structure around the mihrab, the picture is not good, but it looks like somebody has been shooting at it and knocking the bricks off. But unless one considers the destruction of the minaret itself, but that's an invented ritual of those who destroy, it doesn't go to the heart of a desecration, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have two further questions. Would you agree with me when I say that there are wars that are more territorial and economic wars, and there are others that are more ethnic. In the first category, one might consider, since you seem to be a specialist of French history, that the revolutionary wars or the war of 1914 were fought in order to gain the territories of Alsace-Lorraine. If you were to make a comment in this area that you're familiar with, would the principal characteristic of this war be the ritualistic war, religious, which would consist of going to destroy one's enemy to the very bottom of its own symbolism? Would that be a powerful characteristic of that type of war, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: I think it became that. That's a harder question to answer than it might seem. Those who unleashed the war, unleashed it particularly for their own reasons. They had their own motives. They may have nothing to do or not much to do with those questions, but they certainly knew how to mobilise those kinds of energies on the part of their peoples. In the end, yes, as it went on, I think it became more and more that sort of struggle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My final question: You were able to draw some kind of a map where there would be an almost perfect equalisation between a territory occupied by the HVO, which would have a destroyed mosque, and a Christian steeple, which had been maintained in good condition?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I know that my colleague Judge Riad had one or two additional questions to ask. The floor is yours again, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, your answer to my eminent colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, brought to my mind some other statements by you, as he said, in your general part, as a witness in history, apparently. I noted even what you said. You said that there was a message in destroying the minarets, because where there are minarets, there are Muslims. The message was to the Muslims, "We don't want to live with you anymore," and that the message was that they wanted to remove the Muslims from the memory of history, from the memory of the people, getting the Muslims out of chronology. You said the words "and out of the history of the country." These are very strong statements. Whereas, the Bosniaks accepted the coexistence. This parallels, perhaps, what Judge Jorda pointed out in your comparison. Then you also were speaking about the trend towards mono-ethnicity. You think the idea was to annihilate their existence through the destruction of cultural heritage, to annihilate the presence of the Muslim Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what was going on here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whether it's vice versa or not, but not vice versa, in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: It's a horribly contaminating thing that happened in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you're statement really means that the idea was to erase them out of history, to erase the Bosniaks out of history, and that was the purpose of the destruction of the minarets, of the cultural heritage?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: To get rid, physically, of the people, to get rid of them of the memory of the region, and, as I also said, to remove them from the Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So an ethnological annihilation?

utterances.speaker: Dr. Colin Kaiser
utterances.text: Yes, to change fundamentally the Croatian identity in these areas. You have mono-ethnic villages where people may live to together. They may live separately most of the day, but there is an interaction. They are giving something to each other during the period that they are there. One of the reasons for all of this destruction, whichever side, is to get rid of that other person who is in your people, inside of, in the memory, in the way of doing things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Riad. Thank you, Doctor, it was long, but interesting. We're going to now send you back to your work, your very interesting work, and we want to thank you. We will first ask the registrar to have the usher escort Dr. Kaiser out of the courtroom. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Registrar, I would like to move into a closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
